en: The Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha.
Salutation to Śrī Dattātreya.
Salutation to Śrī Vedavyāsa.
Salutation to Śrī Hayagrīva.

Now begins the third section, the Brahmakāṇḍa, in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: Om! To the Mallas he was a thunderbolt; to men, the best of men; to women, the god of love incarnate; to the cowherds, his own kin; to the wicked, a chastiser; to his parents, an infant; to the Lord of the Bhojas, death; ordained by the Creator as the supreme reality for yogis, and the lord of the Vṛṣṇis—Acyuta, together with his elder brother, shone eternally upon the arena. (GarP 3.1.1)
Having paid homage to that very one who possesses the primordial form with the words "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," I shall proclaim this narrative of Nārāyaṇa.
The high-souled ṛṣis, speakers of Brahman, headed by Śaunaka,
performed most intense austerities at the greatly meritorious place known as Naimiṣa.
With their senses conquered and their diet restrained, those virtuous ones devoted to truth worship Viṣṇu, the primordial teacher of the world, with supreme devotion.
Proclaiming the supreme Brahman, the eye of the universe,
those of great luster who knew the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest.
Some worshipped the Lord of Sacrifice with sacrifices; some, the Supreme One whose nature is knowledge, with forms of knowledge; and others worshipped Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion.
Once, those great-souled and supreme beings held a council,
desiring to know the means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
There were twenty-six thousand sages whose vital energy was drawn upward;
it is impossible to state the number of their disciples and grand-disciples.
Those sages of great splendor, who had cultivated their selves, gathered together;
they were benefactors of the world, free from passion, and devoid of envy.
How may the devotion of human beings toward Hari be unswerving?
By what means can all the threefold action of the self be perfected?
Seeing them thus prepared to question him, the wise Śaunaka, bowing with humility and joining his palms in reverence, spoke these words: (GarP 3.1.11)
Śaunaka said:
"The Sūta, the best of those who know the Purāṇas, resides in the holy Siddhāśrama;
that lord of ascetics and disciple of Vyāsa knows all of this."
"Therefore, let us ask him alone"—thus thought the sage Śaunaka;
then those ṛṣis went from there to the holy Siddhāśrama.
The sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest questioned him as he sat at ease.
The sages said:
"O you of noble vows, we have arrived as your guests; you are the host."
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the services of bathing and giving gifts,
by what means does Viṣṇu become pleased, and how is he to be worshipped by men?
"And tell us the definitive determination of reality, which serves as the means for liberation.
Sūta said:
"Listen, all you sages, to Hari’s definitive determination of reality."
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, Śrī, Vāyu, Bhāratī, and the one named Śeṣa,
as well as my preceptor Dvaipāyana Kṛṣṇa, I shall speak according to my understanding.
There has been none equal to Nārāyaṇa, nor shall there ever be;
by this word of truth, I accomplish all my aims.
Śaunaka said:
O best of sages, for what reason must a salutation to Viṣṇu be performed at the beginning of a book? Tell me, O Brāhmaṇa of noble vows, out of compassion for me.
Then why did you pay homage to Śrī, then to Vāyu, then to Bhāratī, and finally to Vyāsa? O Sūta, O highly fortunate Sūta, tell us the reason for this.
Sūta said:

In the beginning, He alone is to be saluted; He alone is the one to be known by all the Vedas; in the Veda, the Śāstra, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, Viṣṇu alone essentially shines forth as the sole reality. Therefore, Hari alone is indeed to be bowed down to.
He alone is the primary and superior one everywhere; he alone is to be saluted, and not Śaṅkara and the others.
Those who, out of lack of discipline, bow down to Śaṅkara, Vināyaka, Caṇḍikā, and Reṇukā— [they fall]. (GarP 3.1.22)

Likewise, Sūrya, Bhairava, the Mātṛs, as well as Vāṇī, Girijā, and Śrī—all of them are indeed Vaiṣṇavas; neither in this world nor elsewhere do the Āryas say that they are not his devotees. GarP_3,1.23 //
One must certainly not perform prostrations for the sake of worldly gain; these deities are not pleased by mere worship.
Having accepted the worship, all those deities grant the fruit [of their favor] by giving something in return.
Having satisfied [the deities] and likewise performed the optional worship (kāmyapūjā) as desired by those who were pleased and had acted according to their own inclinations,
he offered it to the Supreme Deity, Viṣṇu, Hari, who is praised as Śrīpuruṣa and other such titles.

O Indra among the twice-born, these [others] will grant pleasures and their opposites both here and elsewhere, and ultimately lead only to lower states and darkness; therefore, those who desire liberation, such as brahmins and others, should neither worship nor bow down to them.

In the same way, O best of brahmins, even in times of great calamity, all those belonging to the various stages of life who desire prosperity should constantly worship the primordial deities: Śrī, Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Yama.

Those who bow to non-Vaiṣṇavas—such as Brahmā, Rudra, Vāyu, and others—experience great suffering and great calamities, including leprosy, fistula, and other ailments; they are certainly not devotees of Viṣṇu. (GarP 3.1.28)
O lords of sages, I shall now state the intended meaning here; for it is supremely secret and must indeed be held in the heart.
O Brahmins, in this world, the symbol of Vāyu alone is to be worshipped, and not the symbols of Brahmā, Rudra, or others.
At the time of worshiping the God of gods, having placed the image of Vāyu in its appropriate place,
one should indeed properly worship Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who has entered within that Vāyu.
Afterwards, one should properly worship Vāyu and Supratīka with the remains of Hari’s offerings;
those fools who perform separate worship with garlands, incense, ointments, and so forth [are mistaken].
For them, suffering shall arise in this world and the next; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Brahmins, perform some means of atonement for their welfare—namely, the remembrance of Viṣṇu.

Those deluded ones who, with the notion that they are attaining fruit, bow down to the images of Hari, Vāyu, or Śaṅkara installed by heretics such as Rudra— their eternal reward is nothing but suffering.
If the image of Vāyu has been installed by the best of sages, it must indeed be bowed to;
however, if the worship of Hari-Viṣṇu has been performed with the remnants of the food offering (naivedya), there is not even a trace of fault.
For the Guru is the foremost; Hanumān is great and ever devoted to the feet of Rāma. Knowing him thus, as well as the supreme Hari, to be the son of Vāyu, the chief of gods—GarP_3,1.35.
"O best of Brahmins, let this secret be held in the hearts of all;
for those who are indeed Vaiṣṇavas, servants of the assembly of Viṣṇu, they all always bow down to Viṣṇu alone, and likewise bestow meritorious and pure gifts. (GarP 3.1.36)
Those who bow down to Vāsudeva and Hari, and who properly worship them according to their own ability; GarP_3,1.37 //

Those who, by following the path of worldly activity, do not worship the Supreme Divinity or another [deity] during times of distress—they alone are the Vaiṣṇavas, the servants and attendants of Viṣṇu; all others are considered merely non-Vaiṣṇavas.
Indeed, by means of the introductory and concluding signs, they reach Hari, the Guru, even from within;
the wise call those very [texts] the true Purāṇas, for in the Kali age, no one harbors malice toward them.
Since they establish beneficial active duties (pravṛttidharma) according to their respective castes, the deluded always feel envy toward them; for in the Kali age, such brahmins are indeed numerous.
There is no deity equal to Viṣṇu, nor is there a teacher equal to Vāyu;
there is no sacred ford equal to Viṣṇupadī, and there is no devotee equal to a devotee of Viṣṇu.
They say that all other [texts] that establish Viṣṇu are characterized by goodness (sāttvika);
they alone are to be heard in the world of men, and no others, for others bring only suffering. (GarP 3.1.42)
In the Kali Yuga, among all the Purāṇas, only three are preeminent and dear to Hari.
Indeed, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the foremost Purāṇa and brings about the ultimate welfare of men in the Kali age.
For creation is first expounded therein; therefore, this Bhāgavata is remembered as supreme.
In that Purāṇa, they indeed describe at the beginning the creation of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.
O Brahmin, the great ones declare that knowledge exists in both low and high forms;
they proclaim that everything is accomplished by that very [knowledge], for beyond this is the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
After that, they say there is the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, and after that, the one known as the Gāruḍa.
These three alone are the primary ones for men in the Kali age; furthermore, there is a certain special distinction within the Gāruḍa.
Listen, O Brahmins, to that specific detail: the Purāṇa called Gāruḍa is composed of three parts.
They say the first part is the Karmakāṇḍa (the section on ritual action), and they call the second part the Dharmakāṇḍa (the section on dharma). GarP_3,1.47 //
They say that the third part is the Brahmakāṇḍa; among those, this [Bhāgavata] is the last and the most excellent.
O Brahmins, they say that from hearing the third part one gains merit equal to the merit of the Bhāgavata.
When the third part is recited, the fruit shall be equal to that of the Vedas; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Brahmins, the fruit is declared to come from merely hearing the third part, and likewise for one who recites it with understanding.
Because a third part is heard, they say that the merit for one who recites it is indeed tenfold;
superior to that, they say, is the Matsya Purāṇa, and superior even to that, they say, is the Kūrma Purāṇa.
In the same way, they say that the Vāyu Purāṇa alone is considered Sāttvika in the world;
yet, O lords of sages, among those six Purāṇas that are of the nature of Sattva, there is something further to be understood.

The noble ones say that the Matsya and Kūrma Purāṇas belong to the lowest quality (tāmasa), while they call the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa of middling quality (sāttvika); furthermore, they declare the Gāruḍa Purāṇa to be the highest in purity (sattvottama).
The learned brahmins say that the Skānda, Pādma, Vāmana, Varāha, Āgneya, and Bhaviṣya Purāṇas are rājasa in their creation of topics; therein, one part is sāttvika and another is tāmasa.
Because of the abundance of *rajas*, these are said to be "rajasic"; they should not be constantly heard by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Yet, among them there are portions that are *sattvic*, and from hearing those, the fruit is like that of the *Garuḍa* [Upanishads]. (GarP 3.1.54)
The Brahmāṇḍa, Liṅga, Brahmavaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya, Brāhma, and Ādityaka—these, O Brahmins, are said to be tāmasa; among them, some portions are sāttvika and others are rājasa. (GarP 3.1.55)
For these [teachings] are not to be heard in the world of men by those who desire the truth, because they are characterized by darkness (tamas).
Indeed, the great sages who abide in them possess a sattvic portion; for them, the hearing of these [teachings] is like the single foot of Garuda.
They speak of the minor Purāṇas as being eighteen in number,
as well as the Viṣṇudharmottara and the Bhāgavata Tantra.
The Tattvasāra, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise that which was proclaimed by Vāyu,
as well as the Haṃsapurāṇa— these six, O lords of sages, [are the Purāṇas].
Know these to be essentially characterized by sattva; there is generally no doubt in this matter.
By merely hearing them, it is taught that one obtains half the fruit of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.
Also the one named Bhaviṣyottara, the Bṛhannārada,
the Yama-Nārada-saṃvāda, and the Laghu-nārada.
The Vināyaka Purāṇa and the Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa—these they call rājasa; from hearing them, one attains the highest worldly enjoyment.
The wise have declared that the fruit of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the Śaiva Purāṇa, and likewise the Nandiprokta Purāṇa, is equal to one quarter of that of the Gāruḍa.
Those who know the true meaning of the principle of Hari declare that the Pāśupata, the Raiṇuka, and likewise the Bhairava [systems] are characterized by tamas.
O Brahmin, from hearing these [qualities], the Bhāgavata is remembered as the most excellent among all the Purāṇas, just like the half-foot of Garuḍa.
The merit from reciting or hearing it is equal to that of the Vedas;
hearing its meaning is remembered as having ten times the merit of that.
The merit of the speaker shall be twofold, and that of the expounder even greater;
the great ones say it is equal to the infinite Vedas, and the Brahmins also [call it so] because of the greatness of the burden of the *Bhārata*.
Those who know the secret of Viṣṇu indeed declare that this [Purāṇa] is superior to the Vedas both in its meaning and its substance.
In that regard, the noble ones say that the *Gītikā* is supreme, as is the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*.
By hearing those two there, the great ones say one obtains a fruit ten times greater than that of the *Mahābhārata*.
In the Kṛta Yuga, during the six-thousand-year period of the Bhārata [Manvantara], all the Daityas, having taken birth in the families of Brahmins,
will constantly expel some of the inhabitants and establish their own dwellings there.
Having realized Hari, the Blessed One in the form of Vyāsa then composed the Bhāgavata Purāṇa;
having thus fully proclaimed the Vaiṣṇava [Tattva], he thereafter composed that which is known as the Gāruḍa.
Therefore, this Gāruḍa Purāṇa is indeed the foremost, being in accord with the scriptures;
there is nothing equal to the Gāruḍa in revealing the dharma of Viṣṇu.
Just as Janārdana is the foremost among the gods, just as the Sudarśana is the foremost among weapons,
and just as the Aśvamedha is the foremost among sacrifices, so too is Rudra when devotees have been cut down.
Just as the Gaṅgā is foremost among rivers, the lotus among water-born flowers, and likewise the wind among those whose devotion is unbroken,
so too do they say that the Gāruḍa Purāṇa is preeminent among the Purāṇas for perceiving the true nature of Hari.
In the Purāṇa known as the Gāruḍa, Hari is declared to be the subject of exposition;
therefore, Hari is remembered as the one to be saluted, the one to be approached, and the one who is worthy.
Because Śrī Devī is of the nature of fortune, her salutation is prescribed immediately thereafter;
she is also remembered as the Supreme One, the Best of Men, and the Lord of Sādhakas.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, Vāyu too is to be saluted in the Purāṇas and other texts;
and since Bhāratī consists of speech, she is to be saluted immediately after Vāyu.

Since he is declared to be the *upasādhaka* (the assistant practitioner), immediately after that, he is always called "one to be saluted" (*namya*) by the virtuous according to the gradation [of their status]. (GarP 3.1.77)
Therefore, one should pay homage to Vyāsa because he is the author of this work.
Śaunaka said:
"How indeed should homage be paid at the end to the great-souled Vyāsa?"
"And tell me, O observer of noble vows, the reason for saluting him first.
Sūta said:
"Indeed, the mind of Vyāsa is the primary [object of veneration] immediately after that of Viṣṇu."
Since Hari himself is Vyāsa, whose very nature is the wheel of the objects to be expressed,
Vyāsa is not described as being equal to the Blessed Lord Hari.
O lords of sages, I shall also state the reason for this with due respect:
a certain sage named Vyāsa is recorded in the Tāmasa Purāṇa.
Thus, by relying on knowledge, the Daityas, together with their followers, enter into blinding darkness; therefore, you have been saluted at the end [of this discourse].
This which is the supreme secret should be held in the heart without doubt; for it is said that this alone is to be bowed to by the highest beings and is what must be established here.
For that [reality] of the supreme ones is understood through both summary and detailed exposition;
yet they would not know that which is real, since Hari is their very source of livelihood.
Hari and Vyāsa are indeed one and the same; Vyāsa is remembered as being like Hari.
There is no doubt that these two alone possess the status of being the source of subsistence for all.
Because she has entered into the millions of Lords (Īśas), Śrī is declared to be their mistress;
because she is the source of subsistence for the three and because she is to be served, her status as mistress is remembered.
And because the triad beginning with Vāyu is to be served, their status as objects of service is traditionally taught;
for in the removal of the earth's burden, Māruti was indeed the primary limb of Viṣṇu.
Speech in the form of sentences is indeed remembered as the second limb;
Śeṣa is the third limb of Hari, and he is not to be bowed to because of his equality with Hari.
Those who are to be propitiated are declared to be primarily those to whom one should bow;
whereas Vāyu and the others are secondary, and for that reason they are remembered as not being objects of prostration.
Since the names Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others are eternally used primarily to denote Bhīma and the rest, those lords of sages are worthy of my salutation.
Indeed, it is only the state of being bowed to and the state of being the subject to be expounded that belong to others;
all this has been explained by me—what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Subject Matter Concerning the Division of Purāṇas into Sāttvika and Others, and the Classification of Deities Worthy and Unworthy of Worship," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious *Śrī-Garuḍa-Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O Sage, how did the Blessed One create those presiding deities over each respective principle (*tattva*)? For I do not know the sequence of creation nor the distinctions among the gods.
Thus addressed by Śaunaka, Sūta spoke these words:
Sūta said:
"O best of Brahman-sages, your intellect is perfectly resolved."
In this very manner, O sinless one, I shall relate to you that which Hari spoke to Garuḍa when this question was indeed posed by Garuḍa to Hari. Garuḍa said:
O illustrious one, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, please describe the creation.
Once the creation is known, your preeminence will be almost fully understood;
I shall come to know the gradations among Brahmā and the others.
That which has been declared as the means to liberation is said to be its further accomplishment;
having been liberated by Garuḍa himself, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Therefore, he should be known as Viṣṇu in his primordial form, for he is the imperishable Viṣṇu."
O observer of noble vows, this incarnation is proclaimed as arising precisely from [the Lord's] fullness;
for indeed, having attained oneness with the manifold, he rests for the sake of dissolution.
And even in that case, there is a distinction; one must know that it is indeed reality itself.
Whether by perceiving through distinction, or by perceiving through both distinction and non-distinction,
or even by perceiving within that very [reality] the qualities, forms, limbs, and [attributes] such as bliss of Viṣṇu— one shall quickly go to the darkness [of liberation].
O best of the twice-born, those who are conceived as beginning from another person should be known as having the form of Hari, for they have indeed become one with him.
When the dew has arrived, those living beings belonging to me go forth;
O King Virāja, they then exist as Hari in many ways.
O twice-born one, at the time of dissolution they attain oneness with the Root;
but if Viṣṇu himself were to attain oneness with the Image (Bimba), [then all would follow suit]. (GarP 3.2.12)
How could the individual soul (jīva) be a reflection of Nārāyaṇa?
The soul is dependent on Hari and resembles him; of this there is no doubt.
For this meaning of the word "reflection" has been explained in this way;
therefore, one should not contemplate the unification of the forms of the reflected objects with the reflection itself.
Just as in the case of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others, it is their oneness that is intended to be expressed; here, no distinction between the reflected images and the fundamental form is intended.
Moreover, those who desire to know the truth should understand that there is a distinction even in that regard:
by means of a single part, they attain oneness with the images.
They remain established in the state of being alive as a single part; there is no doubt about this.
Those people who do not know the root of the *bimba* are indeed considered asuras.
Hari, who was indeed one alone in the beginning, becomes many through the power of ignorance himself, like a reflection in a mirror seen from afar.
Those fools who speak thus also go to the lowest darkness.
Limitation is said to be of two kinds: that of essential nature and that which is external. (GarP 3.2.19)
In dissolution, the external adjunct perishes; in liberation, there remains the persistence of the other.
For when all adjuncts have been destroyed, how could a reflection exist? (GarP 3.2.20)

For those who are qualified for liberation, the limiting adjunct is indeed that called the nature of consciousness; but for those who are qualified for darkness, the limiting adjunct is indeed the nature of suffering. (GarP 3.2.21)
Indeed, for those who are eternally subject to transmigratory existence, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is considered to be of a mixed nature;
for all, the external adjunct is the subtle body (liṅgadeha)—of this there is no doubt.
Because the Daityas cause suffering, Hari himself is sorrowful;
because he takes on the very form of their various sufferings, he appears in the form of a reflection of the Daityas.
One should not contemplate any mutual difference or distinction between the images of the Daityas and the original form of the Lord. (GarP 3.2.24)
There is not even an atom’s worth of difference between the forms of Śrī, Bhū, Durgā, and others, as well as those in the form of Sītā and others, neither externally nor internally.
Having somehow understood that which is to be contemplated, they proceed to the lower darkness;
for the reflected image always exists in the form of a woman.
O best of birds, when the dissolution has arrived, those who abide as reflections do not attain oneness with the original source, even though they are together with Lakṣmī.
O son of Vinatā, one should not entertain even the slightest doubt that there is any difference, however minute, between the forms situated within the *bimba* and Lakṣmī herself. (GarP 3.2.28)

For when the All-pervading Lord lies upon the ocean of dissolution, having placed within his belly all living beings— whether liberated ones such as Brahmā, Indra, and the hosts of Maruts, or those bound by karma, or even those situated in the state of *supti* (deep sleep)— // GarP_3.2.29 //
Likewise, all living beings who have fallen into blind wells and the like, as well as others who are to be encountered in the Kali age;
likewise, people eternally situated in the cycle of rebirth, and insentient beings such as bears and other animals.
Thus, having gathered all people within his belly, he indeed sleeps perfectly in the waters during that kalpa;
and Lakṣmī, who consists of all the Vedas, though eternally nourished by devotion toward Hari, [remains there].

Though her devotion had already increased, she nevertheless seemed to show even greater reverence as she praised Viṣṇu; at that time, through her gestures and other signs, there was nothing in her that did not manifest Viṣṇu and Śrī.
The Goddess appeared in the form of Paryaṅkā, and Ramā shone forth in the form of Vāsas;
at that very time, she alone was everything, and that single Goddess manifested in many forms and spoke.
You are supreme because you are the highest of all gods; there is no god equal to you or superior to you.
You alone are Brahman—not the four-faced one, nor I, nor Rudra, nor Bṛhaspati.
For the word "Brahman" is primary only for Viṣṇu, while it is secondary when applied to others such as Brahmā and Rudra;
Hari is called "Brahman" because he is complete with infinite qualities.
Because they lack the state of being complete in qualities and so forth, others are not designated as Brahman.
There is no infinity—whether by way of space, quality, or time—in any place or at any time.
When even the end [of their qualities] cannot be reached, what need is there to mention that there is no limit to the qualities of those beginning with Brahmā?
For all time and throughout all space, I am together with Vāsudeva.
Nevertheless, my qualities are not infinite; therefore, the dharmas are infinite by virtue of their qualities.
They exist in accordance with what has been heard and are not contradictory; for they are conceivable and inconceivable in many ways, indeed infinite.
Therefore, we are never able to praise the virtues of you, Lord Viṣṇu, nor those of Hari at any time;
neither I, nor Keśin, nor Speech, nor Rudra, nor the daughter of Dakṣa, nor the daughter of Menakā can do so. (GarP 3.2.39)
Neither indeed was Biḍaujas, nor Pulomajā, nor Agni (Idhmavāha), nor Yama, nor anyone else;
neither Nārada, nor Bhṛgu, nor Vasiṣṭha, nor the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnapa), nor Bali and the others.
Neither Virāṭa, nor Bhīma, nor Śani, nor Puṣkara, nor Kaśeru likewise;
neither the Kinnaras, nor the Pitṛs, nor the Devas, nor the chief Gandharvas, nor even those known as the Tuṣitas [were there].
Neither the lords of the earth nor other humans know anything of Viṣṇu; who else here could be inferior to me? For Brahmā is indeed equal to him [Viṣṇu] in quality, O Mātariśvan.
In detachment, in the state of devotion to Hari, in fortitude, in the vital breaths, in strength, and in yoga;
in intellect, they were equal both during worldly existence and at the time of liberation, and they remained joined as mutual supports for one another.
The great ones say that Brahmā is the ego of food, while they call Vāyu the great one who is the ego of the individual soul (jīva).
That divine Brahmā is not able to exist even for a moment in this cycle of transmigration without Vāyu.
Without him, neither the wind nor anything else can exist; there is mutual dependence and a deficiency in time.
When the Great-Souled One became the regulator of the Mahat-tattva during the gross creation within the cosmic egg— Garuḍa Purāṇa 3.2.45.
At that time, the high-souled Vāyu was indeed unable [to act], for he exists in the external creation according to the divisions of time;
Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, however, came into being from Brahmā after the passing of a year.
When ten years had passed, O Great-souled One, Vāyu then became worthy of worship by the world;
yet there was only a slight deficiency in the creation of gross forms, O Great-souled One, and not even by this much was there a loss of gentleness in these two.
Sarasvatī was born one year after the time of Brahmā’s own birth;
since there is thus a temporal deficiency in her speech compared to that of Vāyu, what harm could there possibly be in her being inferior? (GarP 3.2.48)
Immediately after the wind, speech indeed arose after a year;
as long as there was birth, so long did the destruction of the previous body occur.

Śeṣa, Indra, and Rudra—these three are indeed equal in terms of the power of knowledge and so forth; nevertheless, they possess a deficiency in time, for their lifespan is two thousand years. Or rather, it should be understood that Rudra is like Brahmā and Vāyu, and there is no loss in his essential nature.
O Great-Souled One, regarding the creation of the gross [world] and external creation, I should not even consider any deficiency in time.
O Great-souled One, from them were born these three—Vāruṇī, Pārvatī, and she named Sauparṇī—after ten years had passed; they should be understood as being like Sarasvatī and Bhāratī.
O Indra, O Varuṇa, O wife of Rudra, and others, grant this knowledge always without fail.
He in whom such knowledge exists in this world is indeed a man of wisdom; he alone is the one to be known through the Vedas.
He who does not know the internal distinction that "I am indeed the Knower" is neither a proponent of the Vedas nor a reciter of the Vedas.
As many syllables of the Vedas as have been recited by the twice-born,
so many are the names of Hari, and they are always dear to Hari.
Lord Hari is my master eternally, and I am always the servant of Hari;
all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, are my gurus in their proper order.
And Hari is everywhere celebrated in the Veda as the Lord of these [beings].
He who studies the Vedas while knowing this is the best of the twice-born.
He should be known as a reciter of the Vedas, while others are merely proponents of the Vedas;
burdened down by the weight of the Vedas, he is indeed a donkey among Brahmins.
Both the one who prided himself on his knowledge and the one who prided himself on the Veda spoke to each other at all times:
"The water where Murāri resides is the Veda; it is due to the fault of associating with teachers that the twice-born have become so."
O Great-Souled One, there are thousands, hundreds, and millions of great transgressors in the world;
yet Hari, the protector, always pardons them all simply through the remembrance of his three names.
Seeing him free from all offenses, always endowed with gifts and honors, yet inferior due to his gradual progression,
the high-souled Viṣṇu, perceiving that offense, utters a cry of "Hā Hā" out of a mind of wrath.
Arise, O Govinda, you who are well-known as the Knower of all that is to be known; be fully gracious toward me, you who are called the Accomplished One (Kṛtakṛtya).
O Keśava, arise, you whose nature is bliss, you who are capable of sustaining the creation and its dissolution.

Having created Brahmā, He impels him toward creation; having created Rudra, He impels him toward dissolution. Having beheld the gods such as Brahmā and Śeṣa who are worthy of their respective attainments, grant liberation perfectly.
O Hare, O Murāri, you who possess infinite knowledge extending beyond the kalpas, remain today for me who am devoid of sleep and wisdom;
having clearly perceived through the vision of karma that great-souled one who burns away the darkness whose very nature is suffering.

Since you, whose nature is consciousness, have always cast the Daityas and others into the blinding darkness of misery, therefore they say that you, Hari, are of a miserable nature; O Hari, because of your miserable nature, you are the sufferer.
Arise, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva! Arise, Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Mādhava!
Arise, Vaikuṇṭha, you whose form is moist with compassion! Arise, Lord of Lakṣmī; salutations, salutations to you!
Arise, O Lord of Madhu, Lord of Sarasvatī! Arise, O Lord of Rudra, as well as O Lord of Ambikā!
Arise, O Lord of Candra, as well as O Lord of Śacī, Lord of Brahmins, Lord of devotees, and eternal Lord of cows!

O you who love the Śāstras, arise! O you who love the Ṛgveda, arise! O you whose form is the Nidāna, you who love the Yajurveda, arise! And likewise, O Murāri, you who love the Sāmaveda, you are always fond of the Atharvaveda.
O Ancient Form, you are fond of prose; O You of Wondrous Form, arise, for you are fond of hymns of praise!
You alone bring delight to the sweet singers; arise quickly, for you are the Lord of Kamalā.
Thus praised, Viṣṇu—the unborn, ancient one, eternally bound—arose with great haste.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Hierarchy of Deities Beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The desire arose in me, the god Viṣṇu, to create those things to be created and to liberate those fit for liberation;
yet the power of will has always existed in Viṣṇu, and his such utterance is merely conventional.
Then Hari assumed a worldly form and made that darkness his drink;
they say that form is indeed material (prākṛta), for all those who are ignorant enter precisely into that blinding darkness.
All the incarnations of Mahāviṣṇu are proclaimed to be complete;
that supreme form is complete, and from the complete [form], the complete ones have emerged.
Their status as superior or inferior arises solely from differences in their manifestation;
there is no way whatsoever for superiority or inferiority to result from the influence of place, time, or capacity.
The prior form and the fullness, the fullness that leads to the crossing over of the state of being a word—
having taken that form into oneself, only the fullness remains.
This is worldly convention, such as the removal of the earth's burden;
apart from his vision, there is no other dissolution [of suffering] anywhere through Kṛṣṇa or others.
One must not cause pain to the *tattva*; through that, one experiences sufferings.
From excessive tormenting of it, disease arises for him; of this there is no doubt.
But regarding that which is to be known, the suffering [involved in its realization] must be endured together with the teacher;
him they call a true disciple, and he alone is remembered as the teacher.
Those who engage in a mutual inquiry into the true nature of Hari are indeed the teacher and the disciple, O one filled with joy for Vinatā. (GarP 3.3.9)
Even with the guru, one should engage in laughter that is free from crookedness;
for the disciple is characterized by joy and displeasure, while the guru is characterized by crookedness.
Both of them went to hell for as long as the moon and stars endure;

yet the Great-Souled Lord Hari himself, the tawny-eyed Puruṣa, the Blessed One who possesses prowess, exerted his valor through his own auspicious manly power within his own māyā composed of the guṇas. (GarP 3.3.11)
Garuḍa said:
"O Vāsudeva, tell me the true nature of power; a doubt regarding your power appears to me.
Is power the very essence of the Lord, or is it distinct from him? Speak clearly, for you know well."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O son of Vinatā, that potency which Hari, the Lord himself, deposited in her who is called Māyā—
that potency the wise, who perceive the established truth, declare to be the very form of Nṛhari.
They say that [the universe] is divided, and they say it is indeed primordial matter (prakṛti); this should be understood as being like the lotus and so forth from his own navel.
One should not think, however, that by this much there is any loss of power in Viṣṇu, whose nature is consciousness. (GarP 3.3.14)

O Lord of Birds, if the Blessed One, who is the very embodiment of vigor, or Sudeva, were not present in all places and at all times, possessing all purposes, then he would certainly not be the Supreme Lord or the Puruṣa.
With inconceivable vigor and conceivable vigor, she is of two forms: one in the form of a woman and the other likewise as a man.
O Lord of Birds, both forms possess vigor; indeed, their non-duality should be properly contemplated.
If he did not possess a female form, how could he be the very reflection of the women in heaven? (GarP 3.3.17)
This female form born of Brahman is to be contemplated as its true nature; it is not to be contemplated otherwise.
Know that a neuter being is not to be contemplated at all, for it is produced from that [female form].
The neuter is indeed ninefold as its own essential nature; therefore, regarding Hari, there is nothing further to be contemplated.
O King of Birds, it should be contemplated that within the form of Hari which has become the female image, the form of Śrī exists.
Garuḍa said:
The wise say that the union of woman with woman is useless;
yet, within the very form of a woman, there are always those who possess the nature of women.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, tell me also the cause for his remaining there.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Lord of Birds, Lakṣmī cannot exist as the female form within a form that has become female;
how could the Goddess, who is eternally inseparable from the Supreme Self, [be so]?
O Lord of Birds, she is eternally devoted to serving the infinite forms of Hari that take the form of women, by means of her own infinitely manifold forms.
Therefore, separation from Lakṣmī is to be feared in every way;
for Hari, named Nārāyaṇa, is independent, yet he never exists without Śrī, O Tārkṣya.
She serves the lotus-feet of Mukunda, the Lord, with supreme reverence. (GarP 3.3.24)
Even Śrī does not exist in any place or time without Hari; this must be understood by those who desire liberation.
She, in whom he deposits his power at every moment, is mine and is of the nature of a magical illusion.
Those deluded asuras who speak thus all enter into unrighteousness;
they claim that this so-called "māyā" is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), subtle in form, and not the work of a magician. (GarP 3.3.26)
His conceit should be understood as Śrī; therein lies the application of vigor and their union.
The Noble Ones say that union is directed toward the task to be accomplished; they do not say that this form belongs to Viṣṇu.
O Lord of Birds, how could she, who is eternal through her forms such as Sāṅkhya and whose nature is truth, be of a false form?
That body of Prakṛti is hidden within Him; they say its reality is a form existing for the sake of worldly transaction.
If truth were by its very nature of the form of conventional usage, then how could it be beginningless?
O Lord of Birds, if it were not eternally beginningless, it would not be the cause in its most subtle form.
If [Brahman] exists as a cause in a subtle form, then tell me what is the cause of the phenomenal world?
By the power of ignorance, Viṣṇu alone is perceived in various forms; it is Viṣṇu alone.
"Indeed, through knowledge of the scriptures, ignorance is destroyed—of this there is no doubt—and one attains unity with Hari.
If you speak thus, O King of Birds, listen as I explain the reasoning behind it to you."
For how could ignorance belong to me, Hari, the enemy of Mura, who is omniscient?
Just as there is no darkness in the sun, so too there is no ignorance in Nārāyaṇa, in Hari; O lord of birds, how then can you speak of that truth? Alas! (GarP 3.3.32)
Therefore, I am not a Brahmin from time immemorial if I am ignorant due to the influence of association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Where is that omniscient Viṣṇu, O Lord of Birds, and where is the individual soul (*jīva*) of limited knowledge, devoid of true wisdom? (GarP 3.33)
And how could the Vedas ever reconcile the unity of these two contradictory [views]?
[They declare that] the Creator of the world is always free from suffering, possessed of full power at all times, in every place, and for all eternity.
The individual soul (jīva) is always a limited agent, while the Perfect One (pūrṇa) is eternally of the nature of suffering within the form of saṃsāra;
yet they say that there is an identity between these two opposites through the power of the Māyā of the Lord and the subject of Māyā.
He who always practices malice toward those Vaiṣṇavas who are submissive to the servants of Viṣṇu, by him there can never be love for Hari, nor can there be an increase in bliss, nor liberation.
The master of illusion is always surrounded by servants who are themselves masters of illusion; nevertheless, due to their perception of duality, they are censured and compelled [to act].
By that [perception], there shall be an increase in their suffering, as well as the darkness of the lower realms from which there is no return.
From the Lord of Birds [Viṣṇu], that subtle form is primordial nature; it is eternal, it is ever-existent,
and thus it is itself the ultimate atoms of time, wind, and so forth,
which are of a true nature.
The characteristic of atoms (*paramāṇu*) should be understood by those desiring knowledge, and not otherwise;
O Lord of Birds, the ultimate particularity (*viśeṣa*) belongs to the specific earthly objects. (GarP 3.39)
O best of the twice-born, that very thing which is the ultimate limit of division is traditionally known as the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Garuḍa said:
O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava, O Lord of the Sāttvatas, you are the ultimate atom, the final constituent part of all things.
Thus it has been declared there; yet I have a doubt regarding that which is the ultimate particular (*viśeṣa*), for it is not possessed of parts.
For that which is possessed of parts is not the ultimate particular; such appears to me, though your word is indeed true. (GarP 3.3.42)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Even those humans in this world who are endowed with the power to perceive specific distinctions are nonetheless unable to perceive the specific distinction that consists in His being the possessor of all parts (the whole).

O Lord of Birds, those sages who speak thus call that very thing the "final part" (*caramāṃśa*) or the "particularity" (*viśeṣa*); and others, such as the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama, declare it to be a partless atom (*niraṃśaka-paramāṇu*).
Even though it is endowed with infinite parts, they say that those parts are partless due to the vision of delusion;
therefore,
O son of Vinatā’s womb, the state of being an atom belongs to the atom itself [and not its parts].
O Lord of Birds, within a single portion of that [atom] there exist multitudes of living beings;
and within each of those, the forms of Hari exist; therefore, that [form] is subtler than even that atom.

Whether it be that which is subtler than the supreme Viṣṇu, or that which is greater than the great, there is no distinction whatsoever between them; for that which is of inconceivable form, it is beyond all thought.
The wise know that the absence of a limit of time is the infinity of time; the wise know that the absence of a limit of space is the infinity of space. (GarP 3.3.48)
When the qualities are immeasurable, the wise know them to be infinite;
this infinity is eternal and belongs to Hari alone, and not to anyone else.
Although its infinity in all its forms is characterized by the three marks,
nevertheless, its limitation in terms of space is also logical.
Likewise, both delimitation and pervasion are applicable even to that which is of a single nature;
its inconceivable and marvelous sovereignty exists solely for the sake of conventional discourse.
There is no limitation whatsoever in terms of qualities or time;
for although it pervades all beings spatially, it nonetheless exists [in its entirety] within every single creature.
And no division whatsoever is possible for him, even in the slightest degree;
nevertheless, atomicity exists in him due to his possession of sovereign power.
Therefore, know that his pervasiveness is also spoken of for the sake of his descent;
they know that his pervasive form is the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, for those who maintain that the atoms of earth are infinite,
their mutual distinction must be known, as well as that of the Great-Souled Lord.

There is an eternal distinction between the insentient and the Lord, among the various insentient things, and among the individual souls; likewise, there is an eternal distinction between the insentient and the souls, as well as between the insentient and the Lord.
These five divisions are always present in every state and in every respect;
yet, within such an illusion, the heroic one exerts his vigor.
From that [unmanifest], the Lord Hari, known as Puruṣa, created the three qualities (guṇas).

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Lord’s Virility, the Creation of the Three Qualities through the Means of Impregnation, and the Distinction between the Insentient and the Lord," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 4 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Just as the Blessed One then emitted the three qualities from primordial nature (prakṛti),
Lakṣmī manifested in three forms, known by the names Śrī, Bhū, and Durgā.
The wise say that Śrī is the personification of *sattva*, the goddess Bhū is the personification of *rajas*, and Durgā is the personification of *tamas*. (GarP 3.4.2)

O Lord of Birds, one should not perceive any distinction between forms and their mutual qualities due to their connection with the constituent elements (guṇas), such as the earth and so forth. (GarP 3.4.3)
Those who perceive a difference go to the highest blinding darkness;
for the Person became threefold—he is Viṣṇu, he is Brahmā, and he is Bhava.
To cause the worlds to flourish through *sattva*, Hari Viṣṇu himself entered directly into Brahmā as *rajas* in order to carry out the work of creation.
He is to be known as the primordial Brahmā, but not Hari himself;
however, in order to subdue Rudra who was likewise filled with darkness, Hari entered into him.
Abiding in Rudra, he is known by the name Rudra, yet Hari himself is not Rudra;
Viṣṇu alone is Hari manifest, and both of them are remembered as Haris.
These two manifested forms should be understood as representing Brahmā and Rudra;
knowing this, one attains liberation, but not otherwise by any means whatsoever.
Those twice-born ones who perceive the identity of the forms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, go to a terrible hell from which there is no return. (GarP 3.4.9)
Having entered into the three qualities (guṇas), the imperishable Puruṣa Hari indeed agitated them so that they would become oriented toward the production of effects.
From the agitation of the Blessed One, there arose a great [sound] from the three qualities (*guṇatraya*);
there is no doubt that it came precisely from the portion of the three qualities as they exist.
From Mahat were born Brahmā and Vāyu, who possess the conceit of space;
after a year had passed for him, the twins were born.
That principle in which rajas is predominant is called the principle of Mahat;
one should understand this creation to be characterized by the inequality of the guṇas.
Garuḍa said:
O Son of Devakī, for the sake of knowing the true nature of the Great Principle (mahattattva),
you have described the supreme creation known as the differentiation of the qualities (guṇavaiṣamya).
"O Great Lord, tell me the meaning of the term 'guṇavaiṣamya' (the inequality of the qualities).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Lord of Birds, for the purpose of making known the meaning of the term 'guṇavaiṣamya'..."

Furthermore, O Lord of Heaven, in order to correctly explain that state where the qualities are in equilibrium, there is no doubt that it must first be described in relation to ether and the other elements. (GarP 3.4.16)
O son of Vinatā, I shall indeed show you the collection of qualities and their state as they have become a mass,
equal to that very mass itself.
That dust which has formed into a heap should be known as double [the previous amount], and not otherwise;
O son of Vinatā, it is from that dust which has formed into a heap [that the world is produced].
Likewise, the aggregate of beings is said to be twofold;
for these are born from the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), but the root-nature itself is not considered to be born [from anything].
Since there is no discernment of forms that possess a primordial nature (prakṛti),
therefore, O Lord of Birds, they should be known as born of primordial nature and not as roots.
Thus, O Lord of Birds, the measure of your virtues has been declared;
their true nature, however, has been correctly described to you, O Lord of Birds.
In that regard, O Garuda, within those three groups, sattva alone is proclaimed to be unmixed with rajas and tamas; therefore, it is so called.
O Lord, it is said to be "pure" (kevala) sattva, but not because of its superiority;
at the time of creation it may be pure, but at the time of dissolution it becomes mixed.
O Lord of Birds, O best of the twice-born, there is always a mass of beings that is unmixed, and there is also always a mass of beings that is mixed.
All those who perceive [these] enter indeed into the lower darkness;
O Lord of Heroes, the qualities of rajas and tamas are mixed with the other two.
O Lord of Birds, even at the time of dissolution during the process of creation, the two remain indeed mixed;
even when the quality of passion (rajas) has become a solid mass, it contains more than a hundred parts of the quality of passion itself.
And sattva should be known as mixed [with rajas], not otherwise, O best of birds;
for among a hundred parts of rajas, O son of Vinatā.
That portion which was designated as one part is proclaimed to be the extent of that darkness, even when it is mixed with the dust that has become a mass.
O dear one, the state of the mass of dust is thus pervaded by the qualities of darkness (tamas);
even when the darkness has become a solid heap, O son of Vinatā, the quality of goodness (sattva) still exists within it.
O Garuḍa, it should be understood without any doubt that [the element] becomes mixed with darkness by an amount exceeding ten parts; there is no uncertainty in this matter.
O son of Vinatā, among the ten parts of tamas,
that which is designated as the single part is equal in measure to rajas.
"Even when darkness has become a mass, it certainly becomes mixed;
O best of birds, the persistence of that mass of darkness should be understood in this way."
Garuḍa said:
"O sinless one, I have stated that even when passion has become a mass and even when darkness has become a mass, the portions of goodness (sattva) are indeed predominant."
In this regard, I have a doubt; listen, O Lord of the Sātvatas, as to how many parts of the Rāśis and how many portions of the Rāśis are indeed greater.
"O Lord, worldly convention proceeds to that extent, like [the distinction between] milk and water.
Having heard what was said by Garuḍa, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, replied:
Hari, praising Garuḍa with supreme affection, spoke;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"She who always abounds in the qualities of goodness (sattva) is superior to the mass of passion (rajas) and the mass of darkness (tamas)."
O Lord of Birds, even when mixed, it is not called "sattva";
the wise know it as a mass of *rajas* and a mass of *tamas*.
Just as poison residing within sacrificial porridge or milk is still called "poison," so too,
O Garuḍa, have I described the inherent nature of the qualities.
Now hear, O Lord of Birds, about the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*,
and that which is produced from the accumulated *rajas*, O Lord of Birds.
And that which is proclaimed as the quality of rajas has entered into the principle of Mahat;
when the dissolution has arrived, the rajas remains situated within the principle of Mahat.
O Lord, it is clearly divided into twelve parts;
indeed, when the being has become a zodiacal sign, it is mixed with a tenth part.
O Lord of Birds, O Bird-born One, it likewise exists correctly in one part;
and it is certainly mixed with a mass of darkness—of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Birds, it should be understood that it becomes mixed with a single portion of the mass of dust; it is never otherwise.

O bird-born one, the dissolution of the Blessed One within the three qualities and the principle of Mahat should likewise be understood in the heart by those who have realized the true meaning of reality.
Thus, O Lord of Birds, because the three qualities are mixed together, they call it the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya); know this indeed, O Bird. (GarP 3.4.45)
Otherwise, those who understand [it] go indeed to the lower darkness.
Garuḍa said:
"O Supreme Lord, regarding these three qualities that have been heaped together..."
O Brahman, O highly fortunate one, tell me in brief this truth: how is it that for the Viśālās there is an equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmyatā) at the time of dissolution? GarP_3,4.47.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of beings, the wise know that when the three qualities have become accumulated as heaps, they then exist in a state of being thoroughly intermingled.

Now listen correctly, O my dear one, to the inequality of the qualities (guṇa-vaiṣamya), which occurred previously at the time of creation when the period of dissolution had arrived, O bird. (GarP 3.4.49)
Furthermore, that *rajas* which is mixed with the *sattva* in ten parts,
and which has entered into the *tamas* by a single part— that indeed is *rajas*.
That *rajas* which has entered into even a single part of *rajas*,
in this way, all *rajas* enters through twelve parts.
O twice-born one, with those ten parts of sattva, and likewise with the single part that possesses rajas,
and thus with these eleven parts along with the portion of tamas— so it is indeed.
Indeed, when it becomes mixed, that is truly remembered as the principle of Mahat;
O son of Vinatā, this and the other specific [principles] are to be meditated upon through mantra.
One part is to be known as tāmasa within the principle of Mahat; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O best of men, it is mixed with thirteen portions.
"One should understand it thus, and not otherwise under any circumstances.
Garuḍa said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Sāttvatas, this was previously heard by me from the Four-faced One."
"O Lord, the principle of Mahat arises from four parts;
among them, one part is said to be Tamas, and three parts are indeed Rajas. (GarP 3.4.56)
Regarding this, they say: "The form of Brahmā is known as the imbalance of the qualities (guṇavaiṣamya);
it is declared to consist of four parts, and I have heard it is called the principle of Mahat. (GarP 3.4.57)
"O sinless one, you have stated that it is produced from thirteen parts;
O compassionate one, affectionate toward your devotees, resolve this doubt for me. (GarP 3.4.58)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There is no disagreement whatsoever between what was spoken by Brahmā and what has been spoken by me;
for that which is the quality of passion (rajas) is mixed with the fundamental essence (mūlasattva) in a proportion of one-tenth.
O Lord of Birds, all that combined together is declared to be one part; this is what was called the "part of rajas" in the root *rajas*.

In the second part it should be known as *rajas*; there is no doubt about this. And that which was spoken of as *tamas* at the root, its portion of *rajas* is likewise [to be understood]. (GarP 3.4.61)
The third part is to be understood as such; no deliberation is required here.
Likewise, in the root darkness (mūla-tamas), one part is traditionally held to be darkness itself.
Thus, three parts are said to be of rajas and one part of tamas;
they call that the body of Brahmā, known as the "inequality of the qualities" (guṇavaiṣamya).
Garuḍa said:
"O Garuḍadhvaja, you have stated that the principle of Mahat has four parts, three of which are Rajas and only one is Tamas."
"O Mādhava, O Brahmin, it is understood from your words that the body of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin consists of a portion of *rajas*. (GarP 3.4.65)
"The body of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin consists of pure sattva;
for thus it is heard, O Kṛṣṇa, and this doubt afflicts me."
"Cut through this very doubt, for it is worthy to be heard.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"When the *rajas* has become threefold, and likewise twelvefold..."
O bird, O twice-born one, listen to this: you should know that sattva has entered [the body] with ten parts more than the amount of rajas, even while disregarding it. GarP_3,4.68.
O bird, it should be stated without any doubt that, in comparison to tamas, sattva has indeed entered [into it] as being ten parts greater; there is no uncertainty in this matter.

In that regard, by comparison with darkness (*tamas*), darkness is said to be the eleventh part; the single remaining portion is to be known as passion (*rajas*). Thus have the wise spoken. And now, O great-minded one, listen as I shall describe the parts combined in this manner.
O Lord of Birds, upon the arising of the principle of Mahat, the material cause (upādāna) is to be known as having thirteen parts; the part consisting of rajas is said to have twelve parts.
One part is to be known as darkness; hear now its divisions, O twice-born ones.
First, among the twelve parts, I shall declare the divisions—listen to that.
One part of it is to be known as darkness (tamas); the quality of passion (rajas) exceeds that by ten parts;
and the quality of goodness (sattva) exceeds that by a hundred parts—thus have the wise declared.
O best of beings, listen now to the divisions within that which consists entirely of darkness:
one part is to be known as rajas, while tamas is indeed eleven parts more.

O Lord of Birds, in the Mahat-tattva, the portion of tamas is to be known as being one-tenth greater than that [portion of rajas], while the portion of sattva is to be understood as the remainder. (GarP 3.4.75)
"Since the portion of *sattva* is predominant, the four-faced one is called Śuddhasattva;
and thus, O son of Vinatā, the birth of Mahat has been described. (GarP 3.4.76)
Through the knowledge of that, one attains liberation; but not otherwise, by any means whatsoever.

Thus, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, in the third part (Tṛtīyāṃśa), in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the fourth chapter titled "The Description of the Nature of the Body of Brahman and the Equilibrium of Attributes through the Distinction of the Imbalance of Attributes.
In such a Great Principle (Mahat-tattva), Hari himself, together with Lakṣmī—
The illustrious Hari entered and indeed caused agitation.
From that, the principle of *ahaṃtattva* (the I-principle) arose, consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*kriyā*).
At the time of the emergence of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), one part is said to reside in *tamas*.
O Lord, when rajas exceeds that by one-tenth, and sattva exceeds that by one-tenth, it is called "Good" (sat) by the wise; indeed, this is remembered as my very self.
O twice-born one, at the beginning, Śeṣa was the one who possessed the conceit of the principle of ego (ahantattva);
after a thousand years, those two, the bird and the slayer [Viṣṇu], were born.
O bird, having entered into these principles of ego (ahaṃtattva), the immutable Lord Hari himself,
together with Lakṣmī, caused them to tremble.
"I am threefold— as Vaikārika, Tāmasa, and Taijasa—
and Rudra likewise became threefold, since he is the controller of them."
Rudra, abiding in the *vaikārika* [aspect], is remembered as *vaikārika*;
Rudra, abiding in the *tāmasa* [aspect], is indeed designated as *tāmasa*.
Rudra, abiding in the Taijasa [state], is indeed remembered as Taijasa in the world;
and Hari himself, together with Lakṣmī, resides in the Taijasa principle of Ahaṃtattva.
Having entered, it then agitated [the body], and it became tenfold:
namely, the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—these are recorded as the ten;
entering into the principle of ego (ahaṃtattva) which is indeed vaikārika, Hari agitated it.
O Lord of Birds, at the beginning, the presiding deities of the principles starting with Mahat and of the sense organs were elevenfold in succession.
At first, Vāruṇī indeed became the one presiding over the mind;
immediately thereafter, Sauparṇī, Gaurī, and Jā as well. (GarP 3.5.12)
O Lord of Birds, it should be understood that from the remainder [of the lifespan], those [decreases] follow immediately; their arising occurs every ten years in successive order.
Two others, Manobhimānin and Indrakāma, were born;
Tārkṣya and Anantara are to be known as those who are liberated even while still in the midst of saṃsāra.
Thereupon, O best of birds, he became the self of the skin, who is called Ahaṃkārika; from him were born those whose nature is the hands.
Śacī, Rati, Aniruddha, as well as Svāyaṃbhuva Manu and Bṛhaspati, and Dakṣa— these are remembered as being of the nature of the hands.
Immediately after Dakṣa was born a bird named Pravāha;
he is called Ativāha as well, and impelled by his own nature, he carries [beings] along.
He should be known as immediately following the hand, but he is not remembered as being like Śacī and the others;
from that, O highly fortunate one, the faculty of sight arose from the Self.
Śatarūpā was the wife of Svāyambhuva Manu, as was Yamī;
furthermore, Candra and Sūrya were the four who presided over the faculty of sight.
O Lord of Birds, it should be known that Candra is the presiding deity of the ear;
Varuṇa, who is the self of the sense of taste, appeared immediately after Sūrya.
For those presiding over the organ of speech came after Varuṇa;
likewise Dakṣa’s wife Prasūti, Bhṛgu, Agni, and Tvaṣṭṛ.
In that regard, those high-souled ones who are the restrainers of the organ of speech— namely,
those who were mentioned as the flesh-eaters and so forth— are the restrainers of the infinite reality.
And because of their state of equanimity, they spoke in that very manner, yet not out of pride regarding reality;
O Indra among the twice-born, immediately thereafter they became possessed of [divine] presence.
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Marīci, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pulastya, Aṅgiras, and likewise Vaivasvata Manu.
Manu and the others, infinite in number, were proclaimed as having been born from Upastha;
and immediately after that, O Indra, the proud Pāyus gave birth to them.
Among the twelve suns, one is Mitra; Tārā is the beloved of Jupiter;
Nirṛti is the lord of the corner; and Pravahā is the beloved of Vāyu.
O best of the twice-born, O lord of birds, these four were all born as those who identified with the principle of air (vāyutattva) and identified with the sense of smell (ghrāṇābhimānin).
Viṣvāvasu, the two Aśvins sons of Vāyu, Gaṇapa,
Vittapa— the seven Vasus are thus declared— and Agni as the eighth.
Listen to the names of the *satyas*: Droṇa, Prāṇa, Dhruva, Arka, Doṣa, Vaska, and Vibhāvasu as the seventh. (GarP 3.5.29)
Likewise, the ten Rudras are to be known, and Bhava is remembered as the Root-Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, hear the names of the ten Rudras.
Likewise Raivata, Bhīma, Vāmadeva, Vṛṣākapi, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, and Mahān. (GarP 3.5.31)
The ten Rudras have been declared; now hear, O twice-born one, of the six Ādityas:
Urukrama, Śakra, Vivasvat, and Varuṇa.
O best of the twice-born, Parjanya was previously mentioned as having very long arms;
however, those distinct from Parjanya were said to be exactly five, without a doubt.
"O Lord of Birds, it has been said that Parjanya is equal to the Gaṅgā;
likewise Savitṛ, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Bhaga."
Forty-seven [yugas] are proclaimed for the Mahat;
it should be understood that two more are mentioned: Pravaha and Ativaha.
Likewise, O Lord of Birds, the Viśvedevas are to be known as tenfold;
hear their names: those known as Purūravas and Ārdrava.
Two were named Dhūri and Locana; two were named Kratu and Dakṣa; two were named Satya and Vasu; and two were named Kāma and Kālaka.
Thus, the Viśvedevas are proclaimed to be known as tenfold;
likewise, the group of Ṛbhus is mentioned, as well as the three classes of ancestors (pitṛs).
Heaven and Earth are to be known as these eighty-six [deities];
all these gods were born from the one who considers himself the nose-born.
The presiding deity of space is well-proclaimed as Gaṇapa;
those who know the true meaning of reality should understand that he is the presiding deity in both cases.
Except for Viṣvaksena, all the attendants of Viṣṇu, beginning with Jaya,
became equal to him and were no longer inferior to Viṣvaksena thereafter.
These too are intermediate restrictors of the nose;
therefore, they are proclaimed as inferior to those who hold the ultimate reality (tattva) as their authority. (GarP 3.5.42)
O Lord, he who was conceited regarding the principle of touch was declared to be Apāna;
and he who was conceited regarding form was born as the great one named Vyāna.
Rasātman, Udāna, Samāna, and he named Gandha—
these four Maruts are proclaimed as the lords of the waters.
O Lord of Birds, I shall now describe those who were born immediately after Jayā and the others;
among them, Pāvaka is declared to be the first-born, produced at the very beginning of Pradhāna.
The son of the great seer Bhṛgu is declared to be Cyavana,
and the son of Bṛhaspati is celebrated as Utathya.
Raivata and Cākṣuṣa, as well as Svārociṣa, are remembered;
likewise Uttama, Brahmasāvarṇi, and Rudrasāvarṇi.
Devasāvarṇi, Sāvarṇi, Indrasāvarṇi,
as well as Dakṣasāvarṇi, and Dharmasāvarṇi.
"Thus, O bird, eleven kinds of Manus have been proclaimed; and the seven [groups] of Pitṛs, and so forth, were born."
O twice-born one, listen to those who arose immediately after them, who were inferior to them:
Gaṅgā, the wife of Varuṇa, and the sun-god named Parjanya. (GarP 3.5.50)
Yama’s wife was Śyāmalā, the beloved of Aniruddha and Virāṭ;
she alone, who considers herself the Mother of the Universe, is well-known by the name Uṣā.
Rohiṇī is said to be the wife of the Moon, while Saṃjñā is the wife of the Sun;
these six, beginning with Gaṅgā, were born from the son of Vinatā.
Immediately after Gaṅgā and the others was born Svāhā, the deity of the mantra;
she is called the wife of Agni by the name Svāhā, and is heard to be inferior to Gaṅgā and the rest.
Svāhā’s younger brother is to be known as Jñānātman, named Budha;
this Budha, the son of Candra, is remembered as the youngest of Svāhā’s offspring.
O bird, immediately after Budha, she who was named Uṣā was born;
she, the proud one known as Uṣā, is celebrated as the wife of the Aśvins.
She should be known as the lowest of the wise; no further deliberation is required here.
From her was born Śanaiścara, who is renowned as the soul of the earth.
Uṣādhaman is to be known [as his son], and from him Puṣkara was born;
he is to be known as Karmābhimānin and is called Śanaiścara.
Having thus created the gods who take pride in the principles (tattvas), Hari himself,
the Lord of Gods, entered into those principles together with Ramā.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Deities Presiding over the Principles and Their Relative Hierarchy," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa of the third part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 6,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Lord of Birds, those who identify with each respective principle (tattva) abide in that very principle,
each in their own abode within their own body, for the sake of that [liberation].
They began to praise Hari Nārāyaṇa properly;
for in Viṣṇu, whose qualities are both conceivable and inconceivable, all virtues exist even if they appear contradictory.
"Since those qualities of his are infinite, one by one, where is my power in praising them? Thinking thus, she spoke with her head bowed in shame.
Śrī said:
"O Lord, I bow at your lotus feet; I know nothing other than your feet.
O God of gods, all virtues—whether heard or unheard—reside in you, the Sovereign."
O Govinda, O Dāmodara, having created [the world] correctly and granted me my own abode, protect me;
for there is no beloved person other than you who is so full of happiness for me through this hymn of praise.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of Lakṣmī, abode of the entire universe, you are an ocean of knowledge; where are you, O you whose form is the universe?
And where am I, ignorant? Indeed, you possess power, whereas I am truly ignorant and my power is indeed meager.
O Abode of the World, by Your grace alone, Lakṣmī possesses knowledge, dispassion, and devotion toward me at all times; yet, O Viṣṇu, she never possesses mastery over that [devotion]. (GarP 3.6.7)

O Murāri, grant me this forever: that I may attain only this much—the knowledge of what is to be known and the realization that "I" and "mine" do not exist; O Lord of Ramā, there is no negligence, nor will there be any today or eternally.
Therefore, let my senses always fall at Your lotus feet rather than upon the path of the unreal;
for I am devoid of even a ten-millionth part of Lakṣmī’s qualities, and I have no capacity to offer praise—be gracious unto me!
Thus, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, the Creator, seated upon Tārkṣya, then offered this hymn of praise for Viṣṇu’s qualities;
and the high-souled Vāyu, the god of gods, beheld Viṣṇu with his heart overflowing with devotion.
With a voice choked with affection, his words faltering as he shed tears, Vāyu spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"For these gods are your servants; [they worship] your supreme lotus feet, which are so exceedingly difficult to attain. (GarP 3.6.11)
O Lord of the Universe, O God, I constantly pray for the four aims of human life;
for having seen this, it is indeed the Māyā of Hari that is the cause of all, and there is nothing else whatsoever.
Therefore, O Infinite One, even though I am not a giver, I am eager to drink from the nectar of Your lotus feet—
for the sake of the world that has turned away from Kṛṣṇa, whose conduct is devoid of merit, and who is deeply afflicted by their own actions.
O Lord, your descent is for the sake of bestowing grace upon you; there is no other human purpose for you whatsoever.
Through your most excellent incarnations, you have likewise [graced] the cows, the brahmins, the trees, and the gods.
O Vāsudeva, while sporting, you provide for the welfare and benefit of all, and nothing else;
yet our minds are not satiated even as we recite the nectar-like deeds of you, the crown jewel of virtuous actions. (GarP 3.6.15)
O Mukunda, grant me devotion forever at Your lotus feet, for I am one whose food is never cut off.
O God of gods, may there always be nothing else for me except that [devotion] wherein You abide within the person.
And by your grace, O Great Lord, I am where you are;
this deception within my body belongs to you, the Four-faced One, and not to others.
O Lord, my sleep shall be your salutation; my walking about shall be circumambulation;
and my speaking shall be praise—knowing this, I offer myself to you. (GarP 3.6.18)
"O God of gods, seeing the collection of objects suitable for my worship and realizing that they are indeed images of Hari, I shall always worship those forms of Hari situated there. (GarP 3.6.19)
Whatever sandalwood, whatever flowers, incense, clothing, and whatever food, both hard and soft, there may be—
all this shall always be performed as a vow solely for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
“O Murāri, I shall always revile those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, and I shall protect the true Vaiṣṇavas;
I shall cut out the tongues of those who hate Viṣṇu, and I shall fill the ears of those who listen to them with molten lead.”
"O Lord Viṣṇu, by your grace I possess such power as this, even though I am but a brahmin;
nevertheless, I am not capable of praising you, for I am indeed destitute of even a ten-millionth part of Lakṣmī's qualities. (GarP 3.6.22)
Indeed, whoever should pray for this hymn, may there always be for me inexhaustible joy therein;
those who recite this hymn here in the world are truly Vaiṣṇavas and beloved of Hari.
Those who constantly perform this recitation and always offer it to Hari—for them Hari is pleased; O Keśava, when Hari is pleased, what is there that cannot be obtained? (GarP 3.6.24)
Having praised him thus, the high-souled Baladeva stood silent before Hari with palms joined in reverence.
Sarasvatī said:
"O Blessed One, O Murāri, O Hari, who indeed is a connoisseur of flavor [in poetry] other than through the praising or the chanting of Your qualities?"
O God of gods, who are eternally praised by Brahmā and the other deities, may one attain the realization of sufficiency—
that which, having entered the channel of the ear of a person, cuts through the attachment to the body that yields worldly existence.

It does not merely sever the pleasure of the body; it constantly severs the affection for false houses, fields, wives, and sons, as well as for cattle and other forms of property, and even for priceless jewels. (GarP 3.6.27)
Even though Lakṣmī has been bestowed by you, she does not know your true nature;
neither does the four-faced Brahmā know it, nor does this Vāyu; what wonder is there in this?
O Lord, where is there any power in me to praise such a one as You? Compared to Brahmā and Vāyu, I am always inferior by hundreds of qualities; therefore, O Hari, protect me out of compassion.
Having thus praised Hari, O lord of birds, she became silent;
then Bhāratī began to praise Hari once more.

Bhāratī said: O Brahmā, Īśa, Lakṣmī-īśa, Hari, Murāri! For one who has constant faith in your qualities, as he thus praises you, his mind—which was always increasing toward unreal objects—shall [be turned away]. (GarP 3.6.31)
O God of gods, they thereby produce detachment from that world, and likewise thereafter firm devotion;
and thereafter, O Lord, they constantly bring about the grace of Hari.
Therefore, that [knowledge] shall become direct for him; hence my delight in praising the qualities.
That [delight], once born in a person, constantly cuts through the suffering of saṃsāra.
It bestows upon its qualified practitioner the fruit known as the nature of bliss once suffering has been severed;
and it likewise consumes the sins and even the merits of those who praise the qualities of Hari.
Having understood this, the supreme teacher, the compassionate Vāyu, who is dear to me,
[taught] the qualities of Hari— the expansion of all virtues— which are suitable for me alone and consist primarily of bliss.
Like a kinsman of the distressed, Śiva has rescued our auspicious fame as if from merits;
and by your grace, or the grace of Śrī, or the grace of Vāyu, it remains with me eternally.
Whatever the wind always does, that very thing the god always and eternally does;
the god does not create opposition to the wind, yet he creates opposition to that [opposition] eternally.
The wind does not oppose Hari, and Viṣṇu does not oppose the wind;
by the grace of the wind, there is nothing whatsoever for me, and by your grace, there is freedom from fear for you as well.
Just as there is no suffering and so forth for the wind in its source, so too for the wind and the others;
likewise, both [the wind and Mukunda] are not of the nature of suffering during their incarnations.

The divine Vāyu is seen as if powerless while protecting the worldly dharmas according to the [succession of] ages; however, it should not be thought that there is any lack of power in the Lord Murāri during his incarnation as a man. (GarP 3.6.40)
O God of gods, those possessed of knowledge should not contemplate the suffering of Yama and other such things during an incarnation;
once, I went to a place where happiness was destroyed in order to slay the Daityas.
It should not be thought that, because of this, there is a constant cessation of suffering for me or for Vāyu.
O Lord Madhusūdana, what power do I have to praise Your qualities? O God, I am inferior in quality to Vāyu, whether in the form of worldly existence or in the state of liberation.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Bhāratī became silent;
immediately thereafter, Śeṣa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Keśava.
Śeṣa said:
"Neither do I know the soles of your feet, nor does Rudra know them, nor does Garuḍa know them.
I am deficient by a hundredfold part even of Vāṇī; having granted me this abode, O Vāsudeva, protect me!"
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, he remained silent with his purpose unfulfilled;
immediately thereafter, Viśa began to offer praise.
Garuḍa said:
How can I offer praise to your feet, when my mind is already fixed upon your lotus-feet?
How am I, born from the womb of a bird, capable of praising one endowed with such qualities?
Having praised him thus, Garuḍa remained silent, filled with devotion;
immediately thereafter, Rudra began to offer praise.
Rudra said:
"O Lord, O Blessed One, O Infinite One, that devotion which we truly do not know, may it be mine at the root of the lotus-feet of Śiva.
Even though it is ever present, O God, it does not manifest for me; therefore, out of ignorance, I have done what was contrary to you."

O Hari, O Murāri, what power does my dull-witted self have to speak before You, who are endowed with all-encompassing intelligence? O Lord, protect me, who am forever devoid of speech even by a hundredth part of Yours; grant me both Yourself and Your abode.
Having praised him thus, that Rudra, the best of the twice-born, became silent;
then the goddess Vāruṇī, born immediately after Śeṣa, spoke these words.
Vāruṇī said:
O Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Brahmā, Lord of Manu, Lord of Speech, Lord of Rudra, Lord of men—
I am not capable of praising your qualities, nor is Pārvatī, nor even the wife of Suparṇa.
I am ten times inferior to Śeṣa; protect me always, O Lord of the worlds!
Having praised her thus, O Lord of Birds, Vāruṇī became silent;
thereupon Brāhmī, born after her, began to speak to Suparṇī.
The daughter of Suparṇa said:

O Hari, Lord of the Universe, my voice is not capable of praising your qualities, O Hari, nor is my hearing capable of listening to your stories. O God, who on earth indeed knows that blessed state of yours, which even he who meditates upon your true nature cannot perceive?
Therefore, there is no power in praising your virtues; we are always inferior by ten qualities, O Lord of the Vindhyas.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Sauparṇī became silent;
then Girijā, born after Rudra, began to offer praise.
Pārvatī said: O Govinda, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, I have indeed no need whatsoever for you, O Lord;
nor is there even a mention of you in speech, for he who possesses the form of good fortune is always one alone.
O Nārāyaṇa, your single name alone is supremely capable of destroying the power of detachment and devotion,
as well as the killing of countless Brahmās and the like, and even the destruction of ten million wives of one's preceptor.
"O Great Lord, I am merely the presiding deity over names and qualities;
I have no power to offer praise, for I am inferior to Rudra by tenfold."
"And I am always inferior; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, that daughter of the Mountain became silent.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hierarchy of Deities and the Praise of Viṣṇu Performed by Those Deities Who Preside over the Principles," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa of the Uttara-tṛtīyāṃśa of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 7.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Immediately after Pārvatī, Indra spoke these words.
Indra said:

O God of gods, O wielder of the discus, they say that for one who is ignorant, even to offer praise while knowing Your true nature in the heart is itself an act of contempt; yet for the fool who is eager to praise You without such knowledge, it is likewise so.
Nevertheless, it would have been meritorious for you to have used that name first;
for when one lacks the power to praise those beginning with Rudra, should one then say, "I have none," or what else? (GarP 3.7.2)
In terms of his share of qualities, Kāmadeva is always ten times inferior to Rudra, yet he is equal to me;
likewise, Kāma is always equal to me in knowledge and strength, and moreover, he is my constant messenger.
