Having thus praised Hari, the god of gods, Brahmā—the son born immediately after him, composed of the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra)—stood silent with palms joined and head bowed. Then he spoke.
Ahaṅkārika said:
Salutations to you, who are full of all the hosts; salutations to you, whose form is knowledge;
salutations to the one far removed from ignorance, the Brahman whose form is the eternal truth.
"O Immeasurable One, it has been said that I am always ten times inferior to Indra;
yet, O Teacher of the World, even so, protect me by granting me a divine abode, O Viṣṇu."
Having thus praised the one born of ego, Āhaṅkārika became silent;
immediately thereafter, Śacī, born after him, spoke these words to offer praise.
Śacī said:
"I contemplate incessantly your lotus feet, enriched with the marks of the thunderbolt, the goad, the banner, and the lotus.
O Lord, I remember the dust of your feet, which cannot be grasped even by the masters of speech through their minds."

O compassionate one, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, protect me, who am always deficient in the ten qualities derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) and the vital breaths (prāṇa). Garuḍa Purāṇa 3.7.9.
Having praised him thus, the divine lady Śacī became silent;
immediately thereafter, Rati, born after her, began to offer praise.
Rati said:
I meditate upon the lotus-face of Nṛhari, who assumed a physical form out of a mind compassionate toward his servants—
a face which is the abode of Śrī, which is cherished by the undecaying Rudra, Ramā, and others, and which is graced by a mass of curling locks of hair.
"O Blessed One, even Śacī herself has no power to praise your face in such a manner; protect me always!
Having offered this praise with supreme reverence, Rati remained silent right beside the Blessed One."
Dakṣa, born immediately after Rati, began to offer praise.
Dakṣa said:

I meditate with devotion upon the sacred ford (tīrtha) originating from the feet of the Blessed One, which was sprinkled by the Unborn (Aja) and is worthy of worship by the Unborn and others; from the purification of which issued the incarnation of the foremost of the Unborn, the holy site named Gaṅgā, the most excellent among rivers.
Even Rudra, by the dust of your feet—purified by that very mass of matted locks which you wore—became auspicious from his former inauspiciousness.

O Lord of Compassion, Viṣṇu, incarnation of grace, I lack the power to praise such a foot of yours. Having heard of one equal to Rati, I have not yet attained liberation; protect me, O embodiment of the primordial cause!
Having praised him thus, Dakṣa became silent;
immediately thereafter, Bṛhaspati began to offer praise.
Bṛhaspati said:
"I constantly meditate upon your lotus-like face; O Lord, grant me detachment from the objects of the senses, which are difficult to overcome."

If the soul (jīva) were truly the power within these [elements], and were always the doer, the enjoyer, and the giver, then one's wife, sons, friends, and cattle—all would perish; therefore, cut it off quickly. (GarP 3.7.18)

"O Lord, it is precisely by wandering through the wheel of saṃsāra that I have experienced the suffering of saṃsāra and have come here. O God of gods, I have no power to create anew; therefore, protect me always, eternally, and with truth."
Having heard this, the Sage remained in supreme silence;
immediately thereafter, Aniruddha began to offer praise.
Aniruddha said:
Thus, having abandoned the delightful narrative of Hari, you are constantly deluded by the vulva and the mouth of women;
indeed, like a boar, you are a man of perverted intellect who remains eternally attached to the cavity filled with excrement and entrails.

O Murāri, when I fell into and drank [the water] from that which was filled with marrow, bones, bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, its mouth being wrapped in skin and entrails—O Lord, the power of Your illusion (*māyā*) is the supreme cause for my descent into sin. (GarP 3.7.22)

Mounted upon this body— which perpetually revolves in the wheel of saṃsāra, which is of the nature of intense suffering and devoid of even a trace of happiness, and which vomits impurity through its nine gates— the one of utterly deluded intellect [remains].
O Lord, I constantly pay homage to you, even while abandoning the nectar of your teachings which destroy the very roots of the Vedas,
while always supporting my family, and while living at home without performing acts such as giving charity.
Keep this impurity of saṃsāra far away, and always bestow this divine nectar of your discourse;
for even I am not capable of praising the flood of your excellent qualities, being myself like Śacī.
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Aniruddha became silent;
thereafter, his younger brother Manaḥ Svāyambhuva uttered this hymn of praise.
Svāyambhuva said:
"Indeed, even for one who has entered [your womb] to offer praise, there is no suffering of the womb; therefore, I have attained your most worshipful state."
Mānavī was the wife of Manu, and Yama is the lord of Saṃyaminī;
Candra is the presiding deity of the quarters, while Sūrya is the eye and the regulator.
Indeed, these are equal to one another, having completely transcended the cycle of worldly existence.
"Know this, O bird: [the power] is diminished by twice the flow.
Then Varuṇa began to offer praise to the one born immediately after the Sun.
Varuṇa said:

"In the house of the body fashioned by your own will—whether it be toward a son, a wife, wealth, or various kinds of property—all people, deluded by the meager intellect that thinks 'this is mine' and 'I am this,' sink down into the sufferings of saṃsāra. (GarP 3.7.30)
Therefore, O Hari, destroy such evil-mindedness in me and grant me the state of being Your servant;
for I am always devoid of even half the qualities found at the feet of Manu, O Murāri.
Having thus offered praise, Varuṇa stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
and Nārada, who was born immediately after Varuṇa, likewise praised Hari.
Nārada said:

O Viṣṇu, by hearing and chanting Your name, there remains no other reality for me that is sweeter; therefore, purify me, for on the tip of my tongue dwells Your name, which is higher than the highest.
He on whose tongue-tip the name of Hari does not exist is no brahmin at all; he is indeed like a cow or a donkey.
I do not know your true nature, for I am always inferior even to Varuṇa.
Having thus praised the God of gods, Nārada, the lord of birds, became silent;
then the high-souled Bhṛgu, who arose immediately after Nārada, began to offer praise.
Bhṛgu said:
What seat can there be for you who possess the Garuḍa-throne? What ornament for you who are adorned by the Kaustubha gem?
What gift could there be for you whose wife is Lakṣmī? O Lord of Speech, what is there left for you to say?
Therefore, I do not know your excellent qualities, for I am always devoid of feet, O Varuṇa.
Having thus praised Lord Hari, Bhṛgu became silent;
immediately thereafter, Agni indeed praised Puruṣottama.
Agni said:
"By your splendor, my own brilliance being fully kindled, I carry the oblation sprinkled with clarified butter at the sacrifice."
"Because I always enter your belly by your power and digest food with full capacity, I do not know your true virtues; O Bhṛgu, I am always thus [overwhelmed] by you."
Immediately after that, the offspring began to offer praise.
Prasūti said:
Even sages are always bewildered when investigating the meaning of Your name; even the gods, though constantly afraid of You, remain ever with women.
Māndhātṛ, Dhruva, Nārada, the Bhṛgus, Vaivasvata, and all others—out of love, I bow to Him; salutations to that Viṣṇu, the benefactor. (GarP 3.7.41)
Therefore, I do not know your excellent qualities; what power do I ever possess to describe them?
O Lord of Birds, having thus offered praise, Prasūti remained silent.
Agni is the son of Brahmā whose essence is speech, as is the sage Bhṛgu;
and Prasūti was his wife—these three are remembered as being equal.
Those from Varuṇa are deficient by one quarter; those from Pravaha are twice as inferior;
those from Dakṣa are known to be less than a hundred; and those from Mitra are twice as superior.
Immediately after his birth, Vasiṣṭha, the delighter of Brahmā,
bowed down with humility and began to offer praise.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Homage be to that Puruṣa, the Creator; homage, homage to the cutter away of the sins of the non-existent!
Homage, homage to Him who is born from His own limbs! O Lord, I am eternally bowed before Your lotus-feet.
"O Blessed One Vāsudeva, protect me always; for I am forever inferior to Agni.
I am always slightly inferior even to Mitra. Having thus praised the God, he remained silent there.
Marīci, the son of Brahmā who was born immediately after Vasiṣṭha,
praised his guru Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion.
Marīci said:

"My intellect has been destroyed by Your Majesty through this attachment to worldly existence; my senses have become averse to all that is inauspicious. Yet, for the sake of even a tiny fragment of pleasure, I shall constantly direct my mind toward You, and I shall continue to perform inauspicious deeds."
Such am I, the Lord Ananta, always exactly equal to Vasiṣṭha.
Having praised him thus, O bird, Marīci then became silent;
in that interval, Atri, with palms joined in reverence, praised Hari while suppressing his internal passion.
Your essential nature, which has descended for the sake of protecting the world that emerges from you, is likewise faultless and imperishable;
it is rooted in the true reality, unchanging, consisting of the essence of bliss, and for that very reason devoid of modification.
O Blessed One, that which is devoid of the three qualities (traiguṇya) and yet pervades all things—having entered therein, one truly does not see anything.
Therefore, being like a mere spark, I am unable to praise your excellent qualities, O Enemy of Māra.
Having praised him thus, O bird, Atri then became silent;
immediately thereafter, his son Aṅgiras spoke these words in order to offer praise.
Aṅgiras said:
"I am unable to behold your true form, with its infinite arms, bellies, and heads;
adorned with thousands of infinite crowns and graced by various costly ornaments."
Indeed, I am unable to praise such a form as this, which is infinite and boundless; I am equal to Ātreya in this regard.
O Lord of Birds, having praised him in this way, Aṅgiras became silent;
immediately thereafter, Pulastya spoke these words in order to offer praise.
Pulastya said:
That Blessed Lord Hari reveals to his own devotees the world which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
And [the syllable] *la*: salutation to you, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), who is the protector when one is about to fall into the realms of hell. *GarP_3,7.57*
I am unable to praise such qualities of yours; protect me, O Blessed One, for you are indeed equal to Aṅgiras.
Having praised him in this way, Pulastya became silent;
immediately thereafter, his younger brother Pulaha spoke these words in order to offer praise.
Pulaha said: "The great-souled ones declare that for one who has abandoned the form of desire, the offering of water for bathing, the best of milk, fruits, flowers, and food,
as well as the worship of the Blessed One and the performance of virtuous rites, would all become fruitless."

I perpetually bow down to that Blessed One with a constant mind free from desire, possessing only the thought of surrendering myself to You. O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Blessed One, I have no power for Your praise; I am like a mere blade of grass—of this there is no doubt.
Having praised him thus, O bird, Pulaha then became silent;
immediately thereafter, Kratu began to offer praise.
Kratu said:

O Blessed One, at the time of the departure of life, it is Your names alone that destroy the worldly suffering of saṃsāra; I take refuge in Him by whom one, having suddenly cast off the impurity of even a single birth, attains stainless liberation. (GarP 3.7.63)
Even those who, overcome by devotion to Viṣṇu, utter his name alone as their sole refuge, quickly attain liberation; how much more so those who constantly meditate upon him?
Having praised him thus, O Lord of Birds, Kratu became silent;
immediately thereafter, Vaivasvata Manu spoke to offer praise.
Vaivasvata said:

"Indeed, I was always devoted to the performance of ritual acts and addicted to the enjoyment of women; I was intoxicated by my anus, devoted to the organ of taste, and intent upon beholding you, yet now I am perfectly possessed of dispassion through supreme fear."

O Blessed One, may I always maintain devotion toward this body composed of flesh, bone, marrow, and blood, as well as toward thieves; and toward my teacher, fire, the submarine fire, and the Lord, may I attain perfect detachment from suffering—please endure this forever.
I have supreme power in hearing the rumors of the world, yet I have no power at all in bowing down to Nārāyaṇa;
I have supreme power in following after the people of the world, yet I indeed have no power in traveling along the path to the sacred field and other such places.
O Murāri, there is supreme power even among wealthy Vaiśyas and others, yet alas, there is no power even among virtuous Brāhmaṇas!
Having praised the divine Vaivasvata Manu, he became silent;
immediately thereafter, Viśvāmitra began to offer praise.
Viśvāmitra said:
The lotus-feet of the Blessed One were not meditated upon, nor was the twilight prayer performed; even that Dharma capable of shattering the door-panel of ignorance was not acquired.
You have heard my story, which is skillful in destroying the impurities within; O Lord, protect me always with your hearing, for you are equal to the three gods.
Having praised Viśvāmitra in this manner, the sage became silent;
indeed, the sons of Brahmā abandoned Bhṛgu, Nārada, and Dakṣa.
The seven in number, beginning with Vasiṣṭha and likewise Viśvāmitra,
as well as Vaivasvata Manu— these are recorded as being equal to one another.
They are always inferior even to fire, yet superior to a friend in some qualities;
therefore, O Lord of Birds, listen as I shall recite that hymn born of the Infinite.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Relative Hierarchy in the Praise of the Gods and Others," in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, the third part of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[In the *Śrīgaruḍa Mahāpurāṇa*—8: Mitra was born immediately after Kratu.]
O Lord of Birds,
he began to praise Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe.
Mitra said:
"I, ignorant as I am, bow to your lotus feet, which sever worldly existence and grant auspiciousness for the cessation of existence.
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself knows [this], and neither I, nor Agni, nor the three gods, nor the lords of sages know it."
Furthermore, when even other foremost devotees do not know [you], how then could others?
O Lord, protect me eternally from even the Supreme; I am always indeed inferior to Viśvāmitra.
I am always merely twice the strength of Parjanya; therefore, I have no power for your praise.
Having thus praised Hari, Mitra then became silent, O bird;
immediately thereafter, Tārā began to offer praise.
Tārā said: "But those who practice firm devotion with undivided intent,
having abandoned all ritual actions for your sake and having renounced their own kin and relatives," (GarP 3.8.5).
O Viṣṇu, having heard (or seen) a discourse centered upon you, these virtuous ones listen and speak [of it], being entirely free from all attachments.
"O Lord, protect her who has fallen into their midst, treating her always as a friend.
Then Anantaja, Tārā, and Nirṛti spoke, O Lord of Birds. *Garuḍa Purāṇa* 3.8.7.
Nirṛti said:
"Through yoga, through devotion offered to you,
and through service to those superior in all virtues, people attain the highest goal, O Lord, by means of knowledge joined with detachment."
"By the very restraint of the mind, people go to the supreme state of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Lord, protect me always with compassion, you who are equal to Tārā.
Immediately after that, she began to praise him.
Pravāhi said:
"O son, by your power and through your grace, supreme prosperities arise as a matter of course;
for by serving those discourses which are the elixir of the One of Supreme Fame, one stands upon the path to liberation."
O God of gods, may there always be devotion; yet I am eternally equal to Nirṛti.
Those who recite [this] along with the Bhāṣya and the commentary are proclaimed as the speakers.
Koṇādhipa, Nirṛti, Prāvahī, and Pravahapriyā—
these four are proclaimed to be three times more powerful than Parjanya.
Immediately after that, O Lord of Birds, I shall describe those born thereafter; listen to them.
Viṣvaksena, the son born after Pravāha’s wife, a highly fortunate attendant of Hari, proceeded to praise Hari. (GarP 3.8.13)
Viṣvaksena said:
"If Lord Kṛṣṇa is the giver of liberation, the eternal fullness of bliss,
and if there exists supreme devotion that serves as the means for attaining direct perception [of Him]," GarP_3,8.14 //
Likewise, if there is sincere devotion toward one's own guru and toward all holy beings up to Brahmā, in accordance with their respective worthiness; GarP_3,8.15.
O bird, if you should feel affection for living beings such as the tulasī plant, and if you should remember them, then you will surely become immortal; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus praised Viṣvaksena, the great lord of immense power, the illustrious Garuḍa became silent, with palms joined in reverence and his neck bowed;
"I am indeed inferior to Mitra—there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (GarP 3.8.17)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Praise of Viṣṇu," concerning the deities, mantras, and so forth,
from the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śrī Garuḍa said:
O Kṛṣṇa of great intelligence, tell me the nature of the unborn and the born;
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to explain those others as well in their proper sequence.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The deities known as the "unborn" (ajāna) are those who arise within the various families of gods;
for those unborn deities are indeed superior to the deities of action (karmadevatā).
Virādha, Cārudeṣṇa, as well as Citraratha, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kiśora, Hūhū, and likewise Hāhā.
Vidyādhara, Ugrasena, Viśvāvasu, Parāvasu,
Citrasena, Gopāla, and Bala are recorded as the fifteen.
O Lord of Birds, these and other Gandharvas numbering in the hundreds should be known as equal to those born from the Unborn (ajānaja), both in liberation and in saṃsāra.
But those gods born of my ignorance were a hundred times inferior to those born of my karma:
Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā.
Suketu, Śabarī, Mañjughoṣā, Piṅgalā,
and others— these are proclaimed together as the jewels among the yakṣas.
For these—Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and Cyavana—are indeed born from non-birth; they are inferior by a hundredfold to those born of karma.
O Lord of Birds, after Utathya and the sage had consecrated these as kings,
the high-souled ṛṣis are remembered as being equal to the unborn Brahmā.
Śatarcin is to be known as Kaśyapa, Madhyama as Parāśara, Pāvamānya as Pragātha, and Kṣudrasūkta as Devala. (GarP 3.9.10)
Gṛtsamada, Āsuri, Bharadvāja, and Mudgala;
Uddālaka, Ṛśyaśṛṅga, Śaṅkha, and likewise Satyavrata. (GarP 3.9.11)
Suyajña Bābhravya, Māṇḍūka Bāṣkala,
the teacher of Dharma Agastya, as well as Dālbhya and Dārḍhyacyuta.
Kavaṣa, Harita, Kaṇva, Virūpa, and likewise Musala;
Viṣṇuvṛddha, the descendant of Atri (Ātreya), Śrīvatsa, and Vatsala as well. GarP_3,9.13 //
Bhārgava, Āpnāvāna, and likewise Māṇḍūkeya;
Maṇḍka, Jābācali, and likewise Vītihavya.
Gṛtsamada, Śaunaka, and other such sages are remembered; by the mere hearing of their names, Hari is always pleased. (GarP 3.9.15)
And listen, O Tārkṣya, as I speak:
my wives, the daughters of Agni, are eighteen thousand in number;
for these are equal to the unborn Ajā.
No deliberation should be made in this matter.
Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter Kaśerū was the most excellent in virtue among them;
O Lord of Birds, listen attentively as I describe those born after her. GarP_3,9.17 //
But the ancestors other than those seven Ājānas are fewer than a hundred;
for it is the opinion of those who know the Veda that the ancestors are indeed more numerous.
Immediately after that, O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the kings;
[they arise] from the eight [classes], excluding the one hundred and eight divine Gandharvas.
The attendants of the gods, however, possess a hundredfold greater bliss than them;
indeed, these hosts are always to be commanded by the gods through their own mouths, as it were.
The gods and gandharvas are declared [to be superior], and they are a hundred times inferior to those;
the rulers of the earth are known to be inferior to them by hundreds of degrees.
From them, it should be known that the highest classes among humans are a hundred times superior.
Having thus spoken incidentally, I shall now follow the main subject:
in this way, the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as those beginning with Lakṣmī, are entirely [superior].
Having offered praise, O twice-born one, they all remained silent with their hands joined in reverence.
Thus praised, the Lord of Gods, the imperishable Blessed Hari,
reflected in his mind upon granting them a dwelling place.
This is purifying, health-giving, meritorious, and a destroyer of sins;
it generates grace from Hari and is the means for attaining the bliss of one's true nature.
But those men here, O brahmins, who do not recite this hymn and do not constantly hear it— they are all indeed practitioners of illusion.
Those lowest of men who constantly eat while not remembering [the deity] within always consume excrement that is perpetually infested with hundreds of worms.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hierarchy of Deities and the Praise of Viṣṇu Performed by the Gods," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa of the third (Uttara) section of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 10—
Garuḍa said:
Thus praised by the gods, what kind of refuge did the Lord Viṣṇu, the Blessed One and Master of the Sātvatas, provide before entering into them, O Great Lord?
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Great Lord, I desire to know this;
O Compassionate One, tell me correctly if it is worthy of my ears. (GarP 3.10.2)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Into those principles (tattvas), the Lord, the Great Master, entered;
the Blessed Hari, indifferent to worldly ties, caused them to tremble.
In the beginning, the Blessed One created the golden cosmic egg,
extending fifty crores of yojanas in every direction.
Above that, there exists a golden image as minute as an atom;
fifty koṭis above that is the surface of the earth.
Thus, its parts are proclaimed to be one hundred crores;
and it is surrounded on all sides by seven enclosures.
The first enclosure of the great-souled Pāvaka consists of ten thousand [deities] at the front; the second enclosure is to be known as consisting of ten million.
The third enclosure of the great-souled Hara is to be known as that which is surrounded on all sides by a moat ten times the size of the waters.
Surrounded on all sides by ten times more than that fire,
this fourth enclosure is to be known as even greater in splendor than the sky, O Great Lord.
Thus, surrounded on all sides by those ten times greater than Hara,
the fifth enclosure is to be known as that which is called Ahaṅkāra (the Ego).
O Lord of Birds, the sixth enclosure, known as the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), is said to surround the sky on all sides with a magnitude ten times that of the sky.
O Lord, the seventh enclosure, which is ten times the size of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and surrounds it on all sides,
is said to be the enclosure of the three qualities (triguṇa).
It is proclaimed to be ten times greater than the principle of Mahat;
and immediately after the principle of Mahat, Tamas is indeed remembered as the veil.
It is proclaimed to be superior to the principle of Mahat by five qualities;
and from that, Rajas is known to be twofold, for it is remembered as an obscuration.
From that, the supreme obscuration of the *sattva* should be known as twofold;
these three combined together are declared to be a single obscuration.
Immediately following that, space (ākāśa) is described as being called "unmanifest" (avyākṛta);
and within that, which is likewise devoid of boundaries, the imperishable Hari resides.
The eighth enclosure is the Virajā river, situated between the two skies;
it is five yojanas wide and encircles [the city] on all sides.
"There is that which should be known as most meritorious, the destroyer of worldly transmigration;
thus it was spoken by the Four-faced One himself, O Bird," so he rejoiced.
Having all bathed thoroughly in the river Virajā and cast off the subtle body (liṅgadeha), they thereafter attain liberation from Hari.
O son of Vinatā, know that the crossing of the Virajā river belongs only to those who have direct vision [of Brahman] and go together with Brahmā; it does not belong to others.
O Lord of Birds, for Vyāsa and others who possess direct vision, O Brahmin,
there is no crossing over the Virajā river, because their karma still remains to be experienced.
In this kalpa, however, for those who hold office together with Viriñca himself,
there is, by necessity, the complete exhaustion of all their prārabdha karma.
This is indeed so, there is no doubt; for others, there is no total destruction [of suffering].
Therefore, for them alone shall the cloth of crossing over the passionless [state] come to be.
For those who are attached to them, there is no crossing over the passion-free state; likewise,
O Lord of Birds, because they possess such attachments, there is no destruction of all their undertakings.
Therefore, O Lord, there is no crossing over the Virajā river by any means;
O Lord of Birds, there is no dissolution of the Virajā river during the cosmic dissolution.
She should be known as being of the nature of Lakṣmī, the shatterer of the subtle body (liṅgadeha);
she is fit for the state of Brahman. These are proclaimed as the gods named Ṛjavaḥ.
O Lord of Birds, each of them indeed possesses infinite and distinct hosts; and with each of those hosts individually, they are fit for liberation.
Indeed, there are many living beings who, in every kalpa,
create [beings] perfectly endowed with thirty-two marks, fit for the state of Vāyu;
and those endowed with twenty-eight marks are fit for the station of Girīśa.
The gods are recorded as beginning from twenty-four and ending at sixteen.
The sages are said to be eightfold, and those below them are the universal monarchs (cakravartins),
beginning from a hundred births of the supreme Brahmā.
Thus it is declared that there is direct perception; for in this way, the exhaustion of what has been commenced occurs.
O twice-born one, by means of a single hundred kalpas, one attains the state of Vāyu.
After attaining the status of Brahmā over the course of a hundred births,
O Lord of Birds, he subsequently reaches the abode of Hari after forty Brahmā-kalpas have elapsed.

O observer of noble vows, even for Rudra there shall be direct realization, as well as the exhaustion of his *prārabdha* karma; after forty-one kalpas, he attains the state of being the Residue (*śeṣatva*).
He attains liberation together with Brahmā correctly and not otherwise;
this begins from twenty kalpas of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Even Indra shall attain direct realization, and likewise the exhaustion of his prārabdha-karma;
together with Brahmā, he goes to Hari, the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Garuḍa said:
O Great Lord, beginning from the eighty-fifth Brahmakalpa,
Rudra also attained direct realization (aparokṣya) as well as the exhaustion of his prārabdha karma.
"Thus have I heard, O Brahmin, as spoken by Brahmā to the beloved of Hari;
yet what you have thus related, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, causes doubt to afflict me."
"Therefore, sever my doubt so that it may not arise again.
Having heard these words of his, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words. (GarP 3.10.38)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
There is no contradiction whatsoever between what was spoken by Brahmā and what has been spoken by me;
doubt exists only for those with the vision of the ignorant, but for the wise, it does not exist at all.
"O Lord of Birds, eighty-eight and five [thousand] are proclaimed;
the Brahmakalpa consists of forty [thousand]. Thus spoke the Four-faced One."
Because the principles (tattvas) are to be kept strictly secret, it was spoken thus by Brahmā in the past;
this is indeed how the underlying intention (abhiprāya) should be understood—there is no doubt in this matter.
O twice-born one, those who understand the five hundred Brahma-kalpas enter into blinding darkness; this truth, the absolute truth, has been spoken by me.
Immediately after Viraja was the Brahmin Ambarama, who was likewise prophesied;
he too was boundless and infinite, and Lakṣmī was his presiding deity.
O Great Lord, for one who lacks counting and recitation, there is no gift prescribed for their birth at any time; of this there is no doubt. (GarP 3.10.44)
Then Brahmā, who identifies with the egg, became known as Virāṭ;
having thus fashioned this thought-creation, the Lord, renowned as Hari, [remained].
In particular, O Garuda, having been ascended there by the gods who preside over the principles (tattvas),
Hari remains forever below and above them.
Thus has the account of the primary creation been told; now hear, O King of Birds, about the secondary creation.
Garuḍa said:
"O Hari, you previously described the creation, which I have heard correctly."
O Lord, what indeed is to be known as the *prākṛta* (primary), and likewise, what is the *vaikṛta* (secondary)?
Explain this to me in detail, for I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
From the unmanifest (avyakta) down to the earth, those beings who arise outside the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) are all declared to be material (prākṛta); through knowledge of them, one is liberated.
O Lord of Birds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is to be known as "modified" (vikṛta);
that which is called "creation" by the wise is itself said to be the modified state within the cosmic egg.
Creation and dissolution, as well as worldly existence and devotion, the deities and the foremost sages, and likewise the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ; GarP_3,10.52 //
Existing throughout time without beginning or end, always of one and the same nature, this flow of the world is real; it is by no means false in any way whatsoever.
But if they were to speak otherwise than this, they would indeed be destroyers of everything;
for this flow of the world is real, and service to Hari is its purpose.
Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare:
there is no scripture superior to the Vedas, and no god higher than Keśava.
Those who, abandoning Keśava, the most excellent of all, worship another,
should be known as plunged into blinding darkness— even if they are fathers or gurus.
Now listen, O Lord of Birds, to this supreme account of the secondary creation (*vaikṛtasarga*);
he who understands it correctly in this world goes to the highest state. (GarP 3.10.57)

Thus, in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa, in the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*), in the section on Dharma (*dharmakāṇḍa*), in the *Pretakalpa*, the tenth chapter titled "Description of the Creation of the Egg of Brahmā and Other Portents as Well as the Primary Creation" concludes. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The Lord Hari, known as Puruṣa, the Supreme Person,
Viṣṇu himself, lay within the waters of the cosmic egg for a thousand years of men;
Lakṣmī was in the form of water, and Bhūmi in the form of his bed.
O Bhauṇḍaja, knowledge exists in the form of waves and in the form of wind.
She alone existed in the form of darkness; nothing else existed in any way whatsoever.
She alone existed within the waters of the cosmic egg; nothing else existed in any way whatsoever.
O best of birds, in the ocean of the womb, Lakṣmī praised Hari,
as did Prakṛti along with Hari in his two forms as Lakṣmī and Dhara.
Lying within the waters of the cosmic egg in the form of the Veda, he praises Hari:
"O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you; hear my petition. (GarP 3.11.5)
"O illustrious one, slay the Unborn (ajā); bring liberation to those who are worthy.
For the Unborn is declared to be Prakṛti, which is both the lower Prakṛti and the higher."
Śatatarā is Brahmāṇī, the beautiful-faced wife of Brahmā;
Umā and Śacī are inferior to her, and those who are inferior to them have been fully proclaimed.
O Hari, we never desire the slaughter of these;
for among men there exists the Brahman, and two natures (prakṛti) are established.
One [nature], however, is eternally transmigrating and is denoted by the word "unborn" (aja); the second, however, is that which dispels darkness and is also denoted by the word "unborn."

For this very reason, it is proclaimed in the world that when the elder brother is not honored, she bestows both pleasure and pain, while the other [the younger] bestows only suffering. (GarP 3.11.10)
The attributes such as knowledge and sovereignty belong only to those who are qualified for liberation;
that which veils them is proclaimed to be the limb of darkness (tama-aṅga).

O Lord, that which protects and covers Mahāviṣṇu with respect to the individual soul (jīva) should be known as the Supreme Nature (parā prakṛti); she is remembered as the supreme concealer (paramācchādikā).
Thus, that supreme evil one is proclaimed as Ekā Tamoṅgā;
O bird, she exists only among the classes of living beings, and she is not found anywhere in Brahmā or the other [deities].
The two goddesses are designated as the impellers of the individual soul (jīva) and its presiding authority (adhikārin), like two piśācas; I am the first among them, whose nature is bliss.
In that regard, O illustrious Viṣṇu, you are the benefactor who conceals the one endowed with qualities;
O Great Lord, do so only after having completely released the wicked supreme concealer.
"O Mahādeva, O Great Lord, grant liberation to your devotees, for the Supreme Veil indeed causes us to wander perpetually in saṃsāra. (GarP 3.11.16)
"Therefore, O illustrious Lord, because it is eternal, please remove it; let this be my request. (GarP 3.11.17)
Thus praised, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, though always perfectly awakened, appeared as if awakened,
O Great Viṣṇu, for the sake of testing the ignorant.
From his navel there arose a golden lotus, the support of the worlds;
it should be known as primordial (prākṛta), and the goddess Earth is its presiding deity.

And like the infinite sun, He is said to be the source of illumination; Viṣṇu consists of consciousness and bliss, and therefore He is not different from that—of this there is no doubt. (GarP 3.11.20)
Those men who understand that [the world] is the very nature of Viṣṇu go indeed to the lower worlds, as do those who associate with such people.
O Lord of Birds, the crown and other ornaments should be understood in the same way;
there is no doubt that even the crowns and other such items belonging to Hari exist in two forms.

O Lord of Birds, it should be understood that both those which possess their own nature and those which do not are perceived as such when one's own true nature is revealed; they are not [merely] their own nature [in isolation].
For he created the cosmic egg there, which ordains all the worlds;
at the time of dissolution, being devoid of liberation, he is called "the sleeping one" by the wise.
O Lord of Birds, O highly fortunate one, the equality or inequality of those two should not be known;
for indeed, even the dissolution of Brahmā and Vāyu does not exist.
Supreme knowledge, which is the nature of conduct, is the water for the feet and the offering of honor; of this there is no doubt.
The cessation of the senses is called "sleep" by the wise.
O Lord of Birds, if there were a spatial distinction between Brahmā and Vāyu, as well as between Agni and Vāyu, how then could their state of non-separation be asserted? (GarP 3.11.27)
Therefore, O Lord of Birds, that [state] is not real for Brahman or the wind;
indeed, the state known as deep sleep is similar to the state of dreaming. (GarP 3.11.28)
Understand from me that Brahman exists by way of its primary function;
therefore, O Lord of Birds, this [notion of non-existence] must not be accepted as the ultimate reality.
For those who understand reality, austerity is their eternal wealth.
Śrī Garuḍa said:
Because sleep is the effect of ignorance, it is declared that for them there is no sleep.
"For when the cause exists, then the effect exists, O Lord"—if you were to console me with such an intention hidden within these words; 31.31.
In that case, O illustrious one, tell me how fear and such things could exist for him;
for even if fear and the like were to arise, what loss would there be for us?
Thus addressed, Govinda spoke there as well regarding the cause:
"Fear would be the effect of ignorance, for here indeed the effect has no cause."
One rejoices by realizing Brahman; therefore, indeed, there is deep sleep therein.
For if Brahman were ignorance and the like, it could not belong to him in any way whatsoever.
How might one appear happy? How will he act?
Or how does the manifestation of knowledge culminate in liberation? Tell me this.
O Great Lord, O Brahman, tell me: if that ignorance were not real, how could one listen to it with such great reverence? GarP_3,11.36
Having heard these words of his, Kṛṣṇa spoke this speech:
"O high-minded one, do not perceive his fear as being real."
Fear of me is seen in him, and it is solely for the sake of pleasing Hari;
thus, his bowing was declared to be like that of one who possesses both fear and desire.
O Lord of Birds, for one who has attained even a fraction of that [realization], there is nothing whatsoever—neither suffering nor ignorance; how could such things exist in him?
In accordance with Viṣṇu’s command, he imitates fear;
by that, Hari is pleased, and there is no doubt in this matter.
Brahmā hears [the truth] constantly; he does not become ignorant merely because it is inconceivable.
O Lord of Birds, Brahmā is never seen to be subject to suffering.
Even Brahmā, who might not know [the truth] and acts solely for the sake of pleasing Hari, appears as if suffering; this is for the purpose of deluding those lacking knowledge.
As long as knowledge remains without exceeding its capacity, so long does Brahman exist; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
The manifestation of knowledge is defined as the respectful cultivation of that which already exists, as well as the attainment of knowledge;
this is known as the manifestation of knowledge.
Therefore, the supreme Lord Brahmā possesses no knowledge or other such qualities;
rather, the four-faced Brahmā was born from the golden lotus.
Always engaged in contemplation,
he performed that self-contemplation for the purpose of deluding the ignorant and solely for the sake of pleasing Hari.
Even his volition exists in that very same way, for it was not produced by ignorance;
having reflected, "Who indeed created me here?", that Lord [acted].
To investigate that, Brahmā entered the lotus-stalk.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Cause of Ignorance," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the second part (Uttara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
[Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— 12] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then the high-souled devotee of Śrī Viṣṇu, residing at Puṣkara, having entered into the central channel (nāḍī),
contemplated his own root-teacher, Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond all qualities and non-dual.

O Lord of the Lords of Birds, at the time of reflection, even for that four-faced Brahmā— who is a devotee of Hari and whose devotion is uninterrupted— one must contemplate the mere trace of ignorance.
Just as Viṣṇu possesses the mental resolve, so too does he always act accordingly; O Infinite One, in his perception there is always that which does not exceed his own capacity.
Just as the sky exists within its own nature and the world exists within its own nature, so too does knowledge exist within Hari;
yet even though it is eternally present and ever-attendant, it appears as if unknown to Viṣṇu.
O Lord of the Twice-born, even when one performs [an act] for the sake of pleasing Hari, there is still a certain distinction in that case;
listen attentively with a restrained mind, just as that God spoke and understood.

Those who have been liberated from the Vedas always perceive you as faultless, and likewise, the creators [Brahmās] eternally know Hari’s true nature according to their own capacity, without exceeding it.

He does not perceive the true nature of Hari; rather, he always perceives everything as having a form suitable to himself. O best of the twice-born, there is no ignorance whatsoever regarding that [nature], nor likewise regarding the true nature of Lakṣmī.

Even the Creator does not know [it]; how then could others know it? No one knows the true nature of those two in its entirety. Nevertheless, through a portion of the Vedas, Lakṣmī knows the form of Hari as far as it extends.
O Lord of Birds, as long as the Creator does not know that which is within the scope of his own knowledge,
therefore, not even a trace of ignorance can be conceived in Viriñca at any place or time.
Then, having entered the channel, Viriñca did not perceive Nārāyaṇa as being one with himself;
at that time, the Lord heard the Lotus-seated One saying with devotion, "Perform the two-syllabled austerity."
Having correctly understood his intention, he said, "Perform penance solely for the sake of pleasing Hari.
With his sole devotion fixed on the feet of Hari, he performed penance for a thousand divine years for the pleasure of Hari.
Then Hari appeared in his divine form to grant a boon to that best of devotees;
the God of gods beheld Viṣṇu, who was four-armed and possessed eyes as long as lotus petals.

Beholding Hari—Brahmā Nārāyaṇa—who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, whose neck is adorned with the Kaustubha gem, who stands before him with a most gracious and moist gaze, who is compassionate and subject to the power of his devotees; GarP_3,12.13 //
He worshipped [the Lord] with great magnificence and, out of devotion, held the water from Hari’s feet;
that foremost of great devotees, his soul nourished by devotion, praised Hari, his own Guru.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of the worlds, Abode of the universe, the Goddess does not know your true nature;
by your grace, O Indra among gods, she shall always come to fully understand all the qualities declared in the Vedas."
Nevertheless, that queen does not fully comprehend his excellent qualities in their entirety;
for even if something is not explicitly stated in the five Vedas, there nonetheless exists a special distinction regarding this deity.
Those who desire the truth always discern all the hymns in the Veda, both those explicitly stated and those not stated anywhere;
they know at the outset that here, O Murāri, there are exactly four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda.

O God, these Vedas indeed cause one to know; likewise, having reflected from the beginning upon the Purāṇa, the Bhārata, and the Pañcarātra in due order, the goddess Ramā also always understands the qualities of Viṣṇu according to her own capacity.
For the Goddess specifically recognizes those beings suitable for herself among those who possess the aforementioned qualities, such as Nṛga and others;
she recognizes the qualities of Hari in a general sense, and not eternally through specific details.

O Ramāprā, by your grace and through my own merit, I always recognize the qualities of Hari that are appropriate for me and declared in the Vedas; yet no one else knows even some of those qualities of Hari.
And through your grace and my own grace, at a later time Śeṣa shall know those [beings],
whose slight evil karma is no longer hidden, as well as their many previously known qualities that are suitable for them.
Having understood those very qualities and having attained the remaining ones that were previously hidden, he is then remembered as one who has acquired all virtues;
and by your grace, O Lord of Umā, he shall always possess the qualities of Hari that are appropriate for him.
O Hara, O Murāri, when one realizes that what was unattained has been obtained, then one is called "Hara.
And when, O Murāri, one realizes both my world and your own true nature, then one truly knows you.

O Govinda, eternally imperishable, perfectly full of consciousness, by your grace there is nothing [unattained] for me; for even among hundreds, those gods who possess bodies are devoid of knowledge and remain fixed in sense-objects. Those gods who are fixed in sense-objects are preoccupied with external objects; and those gods who are preoccupied with external objects are always merely prattling about liberation as something other [than what it truly is].
O Viṣṇu, in Your own essential nature as well as in the nature of the universe, there is never anything unequal to You;
for You have no material body, and since You possess no [limited] knowledge, that [knowledge] simply does not exist [in You] eternally.
Although your body is composed of perfect bliss and knowledge, you are eternally and always spoken of as "embodied" by those possessed of devotion;
yet, because you possess no material body, you are likewise remembered as eternally "disembodied."
I am born always empty of the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding this body;
likewise, I am eternally bodiless and similarly always empty of external objects.

The enjoyment of one's own wealth and wife, the enjoyment of the worlds of truth (Satyaloka) and so forth, and the enjoyment of appropriate objects such as garments and garlands—all these are indeed designated as external objects; for they are my natural desires, O Viṣṇu, at all times.

Nevertheless, O bird, I am eternally devoid of desire, whereas Rudra and the others possess desire; they are embodied beings whose existence is directed toward external objects, and they are likewise remembered as being possessed of ignorance.
"In this way, I shall always maintain exclusive delight in the enjoyment of my own wife, and likewise for Hari;
I shall always bear the staff, weapons, and so forth for the sake of Viṣṇu’s pleasure alone, and never for the sake of my own body."

I have no desire for anything other than eternal bliss; therefore, I am always devoid of external objects. My wife, too, is devoid of external objects; though her state is undeluded, she appears as if deluded.
To those who are undeluded, it always appears thus to the wise:
"As long as knowledge exists in me, so long does knowledge exist in Vāsudeva. GarP_3,12.33 //
As much knowledge as Vāsudeva possesses, so much is the knowledge of those who are upright and possessed of wisdom;
however, for those who are ignorant or not upright, the distinction regarding knowledge remains indistinct, appearing only gradually.
Just as there is perception in the light of the sun, so too is my specific knowledge;
and just as there is perception in the light of a lamp, such is the knowledge possessed by Vāsudeva.
Indeed, there is a deficiency in the air consisting of its unclear form; likewise, one should not even contemplate [it as] knowledge.
Such power of knowledge belongs to Murāri, extending to the wind and others until their liberation.
But for those who are upright, such as Pipa, Pañcaśikha, Vāyu, and the others, at the time of liberation there is no delusion regarding the dissolution of the elements like earth and so forth;
likewise, for me, Vāyu, and Gāyatrī, there is indeed no delusion whatsoever at the time of dissolution or creation.
O God of gods, those who know the reality of Hari should understand that Bhāratī is like Gāyatrī;
wherever my ignorance appears, it is always for the purpose of deluding the Daityas and others. (GarP 3.12.38)
"By this, the pleasure of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, will be secured"—having thus resolved his mind, he thought:
"I shall always perform [rites] such as the *praśra* for the sake of deluding the lowest of men, just like an ignorant man."
Just as there is no darkness at sunrise, so too, O Lord, ignorance does not exist—it simply does not exist.
For the sake of pleasing Hari, I shall always practice hearing [the scriptures], for this is the certain purpose of the virtuous.
However, for those who have undergone a hundred births and are crooked,
ignorance is said to be precisely the absence of direct perception even from the very beginning.
But immediately after direct realization, there is neither ignorance nor doubt;
O Lord of Gods, through direct realization it remains forever so throughout hundreds of births.
"I possess full knowledge; there is no need for deliberation on this point, O Lord, though previously, throughout a hundred births, it was beyond my direct perception."
"O Great Lord, the great seers have said that perfect knowledge exists eternally, even for Sarasvatī who has entered into the state of conceptual cognition."
O God, ignorance is indeed not to be contemplated regarding Brahman and Viṣṇu;
however, some distinction exists here that must be understood by those who desire the truth.
In the incarnations of Bhāratī, she is sometimes preceded by knowledge;
she is always of the nature of knowledge and is entirely free from all suffering.
For the purpose of deluding the Daityas, he appears as if suffering through a partial incarnation;
yet he possesses no suffering or the like whatsoever, not at all in any way.
The disappearance of direct perception is observed for only a brief moment; it is not on account of that alone that ignorance is attributed to her. (GarP 3.12.48)
In her primordial form, however, there is no forgetting of knowledge for Bhāratī;
if it is so for Bhāratī, what need is there to mention Sarasvatī?
There has never been an incarnation of Sarasvatī in part,
nor is there an incarnation of me in part, O Madhusūdana.
In the very same way, the knowledge of Hari and Nārāyaṇa exists;
it is present in Vāyu, who is a partial incarnation (aṃśāvatāra), just as it is in the original source.
All qualities such as strength and knowledge should undoubtedly be contemplated;
nevertheless, manifestations of strength, knowledge, and so forth are observed even in the wind.
In the incarnations of Vāyu, there is indeed the complete manifestation and concealment of his power in its essential nature; this is likewise the case even in incarnations through a partial portion.
From power, knowledge, and so forth, up to the fundamental form, all are clearly seen;
yet in the nature of the Tretā Yuga, he does not manifest such things.

O Lord, in whatever manner he manifested his true form during the Tretā Yuga, in that same manner he manifests it while abiding in the form of the Dvāpara Yuga; O Lord, in whatever manner he manifested his true form during the Tretā Yuga... [repeated].
Just as the Lord manifests in whatever form he chooses when Vāyu exists in the Dvāpara age,
so too does Vāyu manifest in that same manner in the Kali age.
Likewise, O Lord, Vāyu manifests himself for the delusion of the Daityas;
those who know the internal nature of Vāyu’s incarnations [attain liberation].
They enter into half-darkness; they are Daityas and not gods.
There is no difference even in the wind regarding the definitive determination of the principle of Hari.
"I shall cut out the tongues of those who revile Viṣṇu;
for that very purpose, the incarnation of Vāyu always exists upon the earth. (GarP 3.12.59)

The contemplation of Viṣṇu, who is full of attributes, as being devoid of attributes; and the contemplation of "I am He" (so'ham) and so forth, which is called the state of being filled with the bliss that has arisen.
To contemplate birth and so forth in a body whose nature is consciousness and bliss;
to contemplate cutting and piercing in limbs that are neither to be cut nor pierced. (GarP 3.12.61)
To contemplate separation and the like from the Goddess who is eternally inseparable is like contemplating affliction, sorrow, and the like for Hari, who is devoid of affliction, grief, and so forth.
One should contemplate Vyāsa, Rāma, and others as sages and brahmins;
one should contemplate the Inner Self within the forms of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others.
The contemplation of the inner [Self] within the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others;
the contemplation of the supreme victory within the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. (GarP 3.12.64)
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of his lineage, he did not consider the worship of Śiva and other rites;
rather, it was Rāma, filled with sorrow, who performed the installation of the Liṅga.
In the black [form] composed of the five elements, one should contemplate the form of Hari;
and even in a manifest place, one should conceive of oneself as being of the nature of consciousness and bliss.
One should contemplate one's father, mother, and the twice-born as having the form of Hari; and one should contemplate the oneness of Rudra—who is not independent—with Hari. (GarP 3.12.67)
One should contemplate the non-difference of Viṣṇu from Sūrya;
Sūrya alone is the supreme of all, while Viṣṇu and the others are his servants.
Such reflections are considered a fault and are called "reviling Hari";
this applies even when [the names] are used for non-living entities, specific individuals, genders, or for the *aśvattha* and *tulasī* trees.
Those who offer salutations while setting aside the Śālagrāma are indeed all unchanging offenders against Hari.
O Lord, those who are eligible for liberation, yet through ignorance regard the Supreme Lord as separate from themselves, or whenever they act in such a manner; GarP_3,12.71.
Then, at those times, suffering indeed departs for them; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those who always perform the bringing of requests during these [times] [attain this].
All those who perform prostrations before lingas that are not self-manifested should be known as ignorant; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (GarP 3.12.73)
All those who, having abandoned the empty Aśvattha tree, perform prostrations [to it] should indeed be known as Asuras; it cannot be otherwise under any circumstances. (GarP 3.12.74)
Those who [offer] a Tulasī plant less than two months old, or a new cow that has not yet calved—all these should be known as Asuras; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Those beginning with the *gulma* age and ending with humans are to be known as the arms of Brahmā;
this entire period, up to our lifespan of one hundred years, is remembered as the single Kali age.
In the Kali age they exist as the measure of the Kali, and at the end of the Kali they exist;
on that day, in the form of Brahman, they go to the presence of Tamas.
Remaining there, they await the path of the world without a doubt,
having been tormented by the practitioners of Viṣṇu’s rites who have cast aside their breath-control.
And after a hundred years, for all of them,
the breaking of the linga will occur along with Kali by means of Vāyu’s blow from his mace.
They all enter into darkness to varying degrees;
there is no need for further deliberation here regarding this cycle of existence, which is even like blinding darkness.
Among all [times], that which is at the very end is undoubtedly Kali;
there is never anyone equal to one who reviles the devotees of Viṣṇu.
In the blinding darkness of saṃsāra, he is everywhere a defiler of the Dharma;
he possesses the notion of knowledge regarding false gifts, and the notion of happiness regarding suffering. (GarP 3.12.82)
Therefore, there is no devotee of Śiva anywhere in the world equal to Kali;
he alone is called Duryodhana, whose very nature consists of infinite suffering.
A hundredth part of that [portion] was always the wife of Kali;
she is renowned in the world as Alakṣmī and is remembered as Mantharā.
Therefore, Vipracitti was always ten times inferior;
he himself is called Jarāsandha, and after him came Kālanemi.
Therefore, that [measure] diminished by one hundredth part is known as a *kaṃsa*;
from that, the two called *madhuka* and *kaiṭabha* are each diminished by five parts.
Those two, Haṃsa and Hiḍambaka, should be known as such, O Janārdana;
and Bhauma is remembered on the surface of the earth as equal to Vipracitti.
Therefore, Hariṇyakaśipu is remembered as being endowed with eight qualities;
and from him, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa was born, who was deficient in three of those qualities.
Maṇimān is to be known as equal to him; Baka is remembered as slightly inferior; and the great asura named Tāraka is twenty times less than that.
Therefore, Śambara, the thorn of the world, was inferior in six qualities;
Śālva, the lowest among the Daityas, should be known as equal to Śambara.
Hiḍimba is said to be inferior to Śambara by a factor of two;
Bāṇa is to be known as lower than him, and he [is surpassed] by the one named Kīcaka.
The one known as Dvāpara is remembered as having great laughter and being equal to the asura Bāṇa;
Namuci, the best of daityas, is ten times inferior to him.
Both Pāka and Ilvala should be known as equal to Namuci;
Vātāpi, the lowest of Dānavas, was four times inferior to him.
Therefore, the king of the Daityas named Dhenuka was inferior by half those qualities;
and the Daitya Keśin was even lower than Dhenuka by half those qualities.
The great asura Tṛṇāvarta should be known as equal to the Daitya Keśin;
O Lord of Ramā, Haṃsa was ten times inferior to him.
O best of beings, he who was equal in three ways in a previous birth is to be known as Tririka; he is remembered as Tatsama, and he alone is to be understood as Veta.
Therefore, O Lord, Kuṃbhāṇḍaka and Kuparṇaka are inferior by one quality each; however, Duḥśāsana should be known as equal to Jarāsaṃdha.
Vikarṇa, the best of the Daityas, should be known as equal to Kaṃsa;
he is renowned as being inferior to Kumbhakarṇa by a factor of one hundred.
Therefore, the great asura Śatadhanvan was inferior by a hundredfold;
the enemy of Karmāri, the best of Daityas, should be known as equal to him.
The Kālakeya, however, should be known as always considered equal to Vena;
indeed, the equality of the lowest Daityas with the highest is thus declared.
And because of their absorption therein, they should be known as gods; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the great divine being of mind and consciousness is a hundred times inferior [to that state].
But one who identifies with that body is a hundred times superior to him;
and a great deity the size of a cubit is a hundred times inferior to him.
Therefore, the great Asura Pādamāna is a hundred times inferior;
however, the one who presides over the sense of sight is superior to him by a hundredfold.
But one who possesses the faculty of sight is a hundred times better than that; and a great god who possesses the faculty of touch is superior by a hundred times more than that.
The great Caṇḍamānasura is a hundredfold less than that;
the great Śiśramānasura is a hundredfold less than him.
Therefore, the Asura of action (karmamānāsura) is declared to be a hundred times inferior.
All the presiding deities, beginning with Rudra, are impelled by the Kalpas and other such factors.
O best of beings, they may at times act in total opposition to you;
but I and Vāyu, O sir, shall never act in opposition to you.
O Great Lord, because the intellect of Rudra and the others perishes regarding the root incarnations, they are all indeed severed from them.
"O Lord of the Earth, because my intellect is fixed upon him, I am known as 'Unbroken-Consciousness' (Acchinnasaṃjñika).
Even though I am such a person, O God, I do not possess the power to grant you [your desire]."
"O Great Lord, have compassion for me, whose devotion is unbroken.
Having thus praised Hari, Brahmā stood before him with palms joined in reverence.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Praise of Brahmā," in the Dharma-kāṇḍa of the second part of the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. [Chapter 13 of the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Thus praised by his own son with words profound as the ocean, the Blessed One Madhusūdana, that treasury of compassion, spoke.
"O Brahmā, by my grace, create these gods in due order;
O Great Lord, create everything just as it was before."
"There is no purpose served by that; create it for my pleasure.
Thus addressed by Hari, Brahmā praised Hari, the Supreme.
Gladdening Mādhava, Brahmā, whose essence is the principle of Mahat, set his mind upon performing creation, [addressing] Vāyu, who presides over the individual soul (jīva).
In the beginning, he who is the soul of the Puruṣa created Garuḍa;
and from his right hand, he likewise created Brahmāṇī,
O highly fortunate one, she who is the regulator of the unmanifest.
From the left hand emerged Satyaputra, the fire whose essence is the principle of Mahat.
From the right hand of Brahmā was born Hara, whose nature is ego (ahaṅkāra);
first Śeṣa was born, and immediately after him, Garuḍa.
Immediately after that, the Lord Rudra,
the great master Brahmā, created [the world] in this manner ten years after his own birth.
After one year, the Lord brought forth Vāyu;
immediately after the birth of Vāyu, he generated Gāyatrī.
After one year, the Lord emitted Bhāratī;
after Bhāratī, he emitted Śrī after ten thousand divine years.
Immediately thereafter, Garuḍa came into being;
after that, following one thousand divine years, he likewise created Rudra.
Immediately after Śeṣa, the Great Lord,
the lotus-seated one, created the goddess Vāruṇī ten years later.
Immediately after Garuḍa, the Lord created the goddess Sauparṇī,
and ten years thereafter, he likewise created Pārvatī.
After Pārvatī, he created Candra, the controller of the principle of the mind;
and after ten years, he then created Vāsava.
Abhimānī was born from the right arm of Parameṣṭhin; ten years later, the lord Śacī brought him forth.
Immediately after Indra, and thirty years thereafter, he created Kāma from his left arm, who is the presiding deity of the mind-tattva.
Immediately after that, the great lord begot Rati, the wife of Kāma, as a goddess born ten years later.
He alone is proclaimed to be the presiding deity of desire;
immediately after the production of the effect, Brahmā [assumes] the vital breath (prāṇa) consisting of ego-consciousness (ahaṅkārika).
Ten years later, he then created Nāsika;
and five years after that, [he created] the wife of that Nāsika.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, fashioned his left nostril;
following from the ego (ahaṅkāra), Brahmā [produced] Sañjñā and Bṛhaspati.
And after two years had passed, he created Varṣā;
but after five years had passed, he fashioned Tārā as his wife.
Immediately after the Guru and immediately after the twenty-fifth [Tattva],
the omnipresent Lord created Brahmā and Svāyambhuva Manu by means of his mind.
After five years, he created Śatarūpā;
after Śatarūpā, however, at the end of twenty years and days.
Dakṣa, who was like a disciple, was born from the right thumb of the Lord;
five years later, however, the four-faced one was born from the left thumb.
Brahmā created Prasūti with great reverence for the purpose of creation,
immediately after Dakṣa and twenty-five [generations] thereafter.
From the middle finger joint, he indeed fashioned Aniruddha;
after five years had passed, the unborn Lord created him.
The joint of the middle finger [produced] his wife named Virāj;
this occurred immediately after Aniruddha, following a period of one hundred years.
From the joint of his little finger, the Lord created the Pravaha wind; ten years thereafter, the Lord created the Pravāhin wind.
And from the joint of the little finger is Vāmadeva, without a doubt;
after that is Pravaha, and after a hundred years, O Brahman, is Ananta.
Immediately after eight years,
the Great Lord fashioned Yama from his back, and from that very same source, he created his wife, the goddess Śāmalā.
Immediately after Yama, and thirty years thereafter, he created Candra from his right ear,
who governs the principle of the ear.
After nine years, however, the Lord created Rohiṇī from his left ear,
and from that same left ear he created Garuḍa, who presides over the left ear.
Immediately after the moon, and twenty years thereafter,
Brahmā perfectly fashioned the sun and the deity of the right eye.
After six years, the Lord Brahmā created Saṃjñā from his left eye;
she appeared after the Sun, one hundred years later.
From the sense-organ of taste, the Lord created Varuṇa and his proud attendant;
twenty years later, from that very same organ, he [created others].
Brahmā created Gaṅgā as the presiding deity of the sense of taste,
immediately after Varuṇa and ten years later.
From his lap, Brahmā created Nārada, who is dear to the Blessed One;
immediately after Nārada, and sixty years thereafter.
The Lord Brahmā fashioned Agni from the sense-organ of the skin;
therefore, he became the presiding deity of speech immediately after five years.
Brahmā created Svāhā; they call her the deity of mantra.
O Indra, after Agni, he created Bhṛgu, the most excellent of the Brahman-sages.
After ten years, however, he brought forth [Nārada] from the middle of his eyebrows;
after another year, he brought forth Bhṛgu’s wife.
Immediately after Bhṛgu, the Lord Brahmā himself, after a hundred years had passed,
produced Kaśyapa through his mind.
After one year, the Lord created Aditi;
after Kaśyapa, he created Atri ten years later.
Immediately after Atri, Brahmā gave birth to Bharadvāja ten years later, and Vasiṣṭha immediately after that.
Ten years later, however, the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) created their wives in succession, at intervals of one year each.
Immediately after Vasiṣṭha, the Lord indeed created Gautama;
ten years later, he then created Jamadagni.
Ten years after that, Vaivasvata Manu came into being;
ten years after Manu, [the next] was born.
The highly fortunate Viṣvaksena, the son of Vāyu and possessor of great strength,
became the leader of the Gaṇas for the Lord in the fourteenth year.
Immediately after him, Vīndra became the lord of wealth (Kubera) there at the age of eight; his wife became so in the following year.
Immediately after Viṣvaksena, and ten years thereafter,
the lotus-seated Brahmā created Jayā and others who were devotees of the Blessed Lord.
Immediately after Jayā and the others, Brahmā created the *karmadevatās* beginning with Vallā;
then, after a hundred years, he created the vehicle of Śiva.
Immediately after the Karmadevas, and thirty years thereafter,
Brahmā created Parjanya, who presides over mantras and yantras.
After Parjanya, Brahmā, ten years later,
begot Puṣkara, who presides over the principle of action (karma).
Thus Brahmā created [the world] through my grace, O Lord of Birds;
knowing this, one attains liberation, and not otherwise by any means whatsoever.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Origin of the Devas," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa. [Chapter 14] Śrī Garuḍa said:
O Hari, tell me of the incarnations, as well as those of Lakṣmī and the gods;
O observer of vows, tell me the distinction between the qualities of my disciple and myself.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O hero, there has never been anyone like Him— the Lord who is the primordial form, infinite, possessed of perfect qualities by Brahmā and the other gods, independent, ancient, whose body is complete, and who is my very self.
The feet were full, the soles of the feet were full, the nails were full, and the hips and neck were full;
the thighs were full, the belly was full, and even having obtained these, he likewise grasped the full chest.
The shoulders are fully developed and all the arms are complete; the hair, beard, and teeth are complete;
the body hairs are complete, as are the pores, and likewise the male organ is complete.
The testicles are full, as are the hairs of the pubic region; the armpits, eyes, and ears—all these are full.
How can I describe the original form of Hari, in which strength is entirely complete throughout the entire body?
Indeed, Brahman exists even within those things that have but a single hair; for He alone is the Full.
He alone is the creator of all, He alone is the destroyer, and He alone is the enjoyer of the essential essence.
Hari does not consume the essence-less parts; O Lord of Birds, listen well as I shall describe the essences:
the essence of grapes, the essence of sugarcane, the essence of the coconut, the essence of the mango, and also the essence of the jackfruit.

Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate and most excellent devotee, constantly takes the essence of the orange, the essence of the betel nut, the essence of the date palm, the essence of the plantain fruit, and the essence of the seed-form.
The essence of betel, the essence of khadira wood, the essence of flowers, and the essence of sandalwood;
the essence of wheat, the essence of barley, the essence of black gram, and the essence of hareṇu beans.
Likewise, pure rice, the essence of nīvāra, the essence of śyāmāka, and the essence of pure grain; 10.10 //

Viṣṇu accepts with supreme reverence the essence of all prohibited vegetables as well as the essence of prohibited salts; he accepts the essence of food and the essence of what is fit to be eaten or consumed.
Viṣṇu takes the essence of soup, the essence of fine rice, the essence of milk, the essence of curd and buttermilk,
the essence of clarified butter, the essence of asafoetida, and even the essence of mustard seed.

The essence of black pepper, the essence of cumin, likewise the essence of sacrificial oblation cooked in ghee, the essence of that which is fried in oils, the essence of roasted jaggery, and the essence of fresh butter; GarP_3.14.13.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of Lakṣmī and the dweller of all the worlds, eats the essence of cloves, the essence of sugar, and other such essences; and by his command, Vāsudeva also eats them constantly.
O best of disciples, hear also of the portions of the Great-Souled One that remain as the essence of those [others];
for when even these are thus deluded regarding Vāsudeva, what more need be said of those who are devotees of Viṣṇu in this world?
Blessed are those who consume the essence; for them, there shall be no increase of suffering.
Know that those who eat the *vaiśvadeva* offering while neglecting it—those wicked ones who merely think of eating—are truly wretched.
O Lord of Birds, I shall declare the specific details regarding the Vaiśvadeva offering—something that a wise man should not speak elsewhere except to one who is generous.
Regarding the offerings to the Sun and the other deities, one should present them, excluding Vāyu and Hari who resides within.
They indeed should always be known as consumers of the essence alone; therefore, Viṣṇu is the one Great Soul.
He is the consumer of the essential portion, but not the consumer of everything; yet, possessing unopposed power, he enjoys all things without contradiction.
I shall further declare other essential matters; O Lord of Birds, listen with supreme reverence to this secret.
Grapes and all such things are indeed without essence, as are those substances that are corrupted by time and the like, or corrupted in their nature.
But immediately after being over-ripe, and likewise during the four days [following], they are known to be pithless and turbid; such is the jambu fruit remembered [to be].
O Lord of Sages, after one month, the panasa fruit is considered sapless; O Lord of Sages, after six months, the kharjūra fruit is considered as bitter as a medicinal herb.
O Lord, a coconut that is fresh and pure is [beneficial] immediately after being cracked open;
however, after a day and night has passed, it is proclaimed to be devoid of essence.
Just as a coconut or a date becomes dry,
so too is the mango proclaimed to be sapless immediately after its fortnight.
O Lord of Heroes, betel nut is prescribed after a year;
O Lord of Heroes, betel leaf is proclaimed [to be used] after a ghaṭikā.
O Lord of the Twice-born, immediately following that, food consisting of rice with soup, milk-rice,
and boiled delicacies is proclaimed to be without essence.
It is likewise recorded that after three fortnights, it is cooked in oil;
and after four watches, it is cooked in ghee, though it is then considered sapless.
After three watches of the night have passed, vegetables are declared to be devoid of essence;
likewise are the citron, ginger, the *dhātrī* fruit, camphor, and the mango.
O Vīndra, after a year it is proclaimed to be sapless;
the parpaṭa is proclaimed to be sapless in merely a fortnight.
O twice-born one, Tulasī is always the essence, even on the Ekādaśī day;
whether it be fresh or dry, it is remembered that the fresh one is the most substantial.
On the eleventh day, the wise should take the essence of the *tulasī* plant with their sense of touch,
but not with their sense of smell, nor indeed with their sense of taste.
O Lord of Birds, on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the food of Hari is proclaimed to be essence-less;
yet on the eleventh day, the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Hari belongs to human beings.
O highly fortunate one, on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) becomes essential even once, and even more so twice, when it is mixed with perfumes and other offerings.
That which is mixed with sour gruel is declared to be essence-less;
however, on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the essence for Hari consists of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
"It is the opinion of those who know the Vedas that there is no essence in the lords of men;
O Garuḍa, in the month of Āṣāḍha, the Śāka tree is said to be without essence."
O Lord of the Gods, in the month of Bhādrapada, curd is said to be essence-less;
indeed, in the month of Āśvina, milk is proclaimed to be essence-less.
Those who are devoid of the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and the mace (*gadā*) are sung of as "not noble" (*anārya*);
for those who are bereft of devotion to Hari are proclaimed to be *asuras*.
A mouth devoid of the names of Hari is said to be essence-less;
likewise, food cooked without the offering to Hari is said to be essence-less.
The *atasī* flower is said to be sapless after three days;
the *mallikā* remains sapful for one watch (*prahara*), while the *jātī* remains so for half a watch.
The *śatapatra* lasts for three watches (*yāma*), while the *karavīra* lasts day and night;
the essence of the *pārijāta*, O Lord of Birds, lasts for the duration of one *ghaṭikā*.
Saffron that is three years old is called *phalga* or *sāra* by the wise;
musk is ten years old, while camphor is only one year old.
Sandalwood is always declared to be "with essence" (sasāra);
now listen, O Lord of Birds, as I describe those that are pure but devoid of essence.
Tuṣā, medhyā, āranāla, puṇyaka, bhiḥ, saṭā, as well as upodvrajī, alābū, and bṛhatkośātakī; // GarP_3,14.42 //
O twice-born ones, eggplant, sorrel, bilva, udumbara, fried grain, garlic, stalks, and likewise kalañja— these are forbidden.
All of this is proclaimed to be devoid of essence at all times,
except on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], when the Vaiśvadeva rite, the Śrāddha, and the libation (tarpaṇa) are indeed performed.
The cremation of a *preta* by means of a mantra is proclaimed to be without essence;
for the deity Nārāyaṇa does not accept these impure oblations.
Hari himself does not seize, does not seize, does not seize;
nevertheless, he knows all the evil deeds of living beings.
Hari causes others to experience enjoyment, yet He Himself does not enjoy;
indeed, the fruit born of the karma of living beings is like food devoid of essence.
Living beings are eaters of secondary food, while Kuntī and others are eaters of primary food;
Viṣṇu drinks only what is auspicious, for the omnipresent Lord does not drink what is inauspicious.
Who could describe his activities? Hari himself is full bliss;
there is no one equal to him anywhere in space or time.
O best of the lords of birds, listen as I shall speak of his incarnations. 3,14.49.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Discernment of Essential and Non-Essential Matters for the Purpose of Vaiśvadeva," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa— Chapter 15—
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, when the high-souled Hari, known as Puruṣa, had gone to perform meditation,
Viṣṇu himself— the ocean of all excellent qualities and the primordial seed— manifested there.
That Viṣṇu, who is called Puruṣa and exists as the seed, became the high-souled Vāsudeva;
he existed as the primordial form within the Māyā of the wind called Puruṣa in order to effect creation.
He who is Vāsudeva is indeed born as he who is named Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose nature consists of all excellent qualities;
for the purpose of performing creation, that Supreme Self of perfect consciousness [becomes] Jayā, who is like a thread for the wind.
He who is known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa is indeed that same one renowned as Pradyumna;
for the sake of producing Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, he himself became the primordial form of the Goddess.

Having created the Great Principle (mahattattva) in its subtle form, endowed with sixteen digits (kalās), that very God sported with it along with the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra). Listen indeed to what those sixteen digits are called.
The elements, the five organs of action, the organs of knowledge, and likewise the mind—
having gathered these along with the individual souls, he whose power is perfectly full became known as Aniruddha.
Thus, O Lord of Gods, that Lord created all the gods, beginning with Viriñci, by means of a gross body;
likewise, Viṣṇu, who is designated as Puruṣa, attained the state of Sanatkumāra.

In order to practice celibacy that cannot be achieved by any other means and for the perpetual drying up of the ten senses, Kumāra was recited at the beginning [of the hymn] by Sanandana and others; therefore, there is no one else here, and no further deliberation is required.
That very Viṣṇu indeed assumed the form of a boar to lift up the earth and to slay the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa;
likewise, O Lord of Birds, the God took that form for the sake of establishing the earth and protecting the virtuous.
Then Hari, that Great Soul who attained the state of being my servant through the wife of the sage Yāminī,
was not able, in that incarnation, to bestow the entire Pañcarātra independently.
That very Viṣṇu became known as Nārāyaṇa upon the earth, the remover of impurities;
he did so to perform penance, to instruct the sages, and indeed to humble a thousand celestial nymphs.
Then the Great-Souled Hari, having assumed the form of Kapila, taught the twenty-four principles— which had been obscured by the power of time— to Āsuri, intending to uproot all doubt.
That very Supreme Self, the Giver, became Atri in form through Rameśā and Sūyā;
that Great-Souled One bestowed upon him named Alarka the science of sound reasoning called Ānvīkṣikī.
He alone, whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss, was born in the lineage of Vaṃśa and Draviṇa through Ākūti;
O Lord of Heroes, he protected the Svāyambhuva Manvantara together with the gods.
He himself, O Lord of Heroes, became Viṣṇu, the Wide-striding One, in the lineage of Nābhi through Merudevī, the daughter of Āgnīdhra;
