a crocodile, a fish, or even a *trivikrama* [image] should be given by one desiring prosperity at this sacred ford, O lady of excellent complexion.
Resembling the shape of a jambu fruit, with a fine tip and marked by dots;
it has three wheels on its face and a wheel upon its tail.
The form of the Fish is described as being enriched with the Śrīvatsa mark and rows of dots; that which is joined with a disc below the tail is described as the Śiśumāra (Pigmy Crocodile).
If it is joined with a curved disc, it is declared to be Trivikrama;
having heard the characteristics of these [images] at the supreme Vāruṇa Tīrtha.

Having obtained this fruit of giving, one rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu. O beautiful lady, in whichever house the aforementioned forms reside, the Bhāgīrathī, the best of holy places, is present there; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, bathing in the Puṣkariṇī is difficult for men in the Kali age;
indeed, bathing in the sacred sites situated there is also exceedingly difficult.
The gift of a Śālagrāma stone is likewise remembered as difficult to accomplish;
on the banks of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the gift of a daughter in marriage is exceedingly difficult to achieve.
The gift of a Kapila cow is difficult to accomplish, and the gift of food is even more difficult to accomplish at the Svāmipuṣkariṇī tīrtha and other sacred fords, O beautiful lady.
"Perform your bath according to the prescribed rule, and likewise perform the gift of a bed," thus was the maiden addressed by the sage Jaigīṣavya.
Observing her vows, she performed the ritual bath at Svāmipuṣkariṇī;
having bathed well in these sacred fords, the beautiful woman made offerings.
She dwelt there for twenty-one days;
whoever hears of the greatness of the banks of Svāmipuṣkariṇī attains supreme devotion to Śrīnivāsa, who pervades the universe.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Vyaṅkaṭagiri, the Sacred Tirthas such as Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the Deities Residing Therein, the Characteristics of Their Śālagrāmas, and the Gift of Them," in the Brahmakāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa. — Śrī Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa 27.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then,
desiring to bathe in the Nandā river which wards off sin, that wise woman,
bowing low with humility, questioned her preceptor, the Brahmin.
"O Brahmin, what is the name of this river, and what purpose do I have here? Tell me.
Thus addressed, Jaigīṣavya spoke these words: ||| GarP_3,27.2 |||
Jaigīṣavya said:
Listen, O blessed lady, I shall proclaim this greatness that destroys sin;
O highly fortunate one, this river is always a destroyer of evil.
The flood of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin is destroyed by bathing here;
indeed, it is seen directly by those who have prepared themselves to perform the bath.
And water appears turbid due to sins;
O Goddess, one should perform the ritual bath only as long as the water is clear.
As long as pure water has not arrived, evil is not destroyed;
once pure water has arrived, it is certain that evil is destroyed.
O large-eyed one, such is the greatness seen on earth at Kalāvittha;
here one should perform ablutions and bestow the highest gifts. Then, having attained knowledge, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Candra fell [from his status] due to approaching the wife of his guru; Hari went [to the earth] because of [his desire for] Ahalyā;
Śukra [fell] from drinking liquor, and Bali from the theft of gold. (GarP 3.27.8)
O beautiful lady, Rudra was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, the Naga from stealing what was given, and Rāma from the slaughter of a Sūta; indeed, they were all released from these here.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to this;
perform your ablutions here, O highly fortunate lady, for by this you shall indeed attain perfection.
Together with her father, the sage Jaigīṣavya,
the beautiful maiden performed her ablutions according to the prescribed rites and then arose.
For as long as the *puruṣasūkta* lasts, it indeed remains;
thereafter, one should recite the supreme great mantra known by the name Veṅkaṭeśa.
Having gratified the twice-born with garments, wealth, ornaments, and other gifts,
the goddess departed from there for the supreme Kamārī-tīrtha.
Having heard of the greatness of Kumārī, that goddess bathed; then, returning, she indeed crossed the Virajā river on her way.
Having seen him, that goddess questioned her lord and teacher Jaigīṣavya: "O best of Brahmins, who is this person? Tell me, what is the purpose here? (GarP 3.27.15)
Thus questioned, Jaigīṣavya, that ocean of compassion, spoke:
"O daughter, this Bhāgīrathī is indeed coming through the middle."
Therefore, she is indeed called the "Internal Gaṅgā" by the supreme ṛṣis;
O daughters, her water is always dear to the abode of Śrī.
Whoever performs a bath here attains the supreme goal;
that maiden performed her bath in the supremely purifying water.
Having thus understood the nature of charity and the other virtues, she recited the supreme mantra;
then the beautiful woman returned once more to the presence of Śrīnivāsa.
Having gratified the Brahmins and others with garments, perfumes, ornaments, and other gifts, he performed a circumambulation limb by limb around Veṅkaṭanāyaka with devotion.
Again, on the following morning, having bathed in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the illustrious lady went to the place known as Tuṃburu.
The Goddess asked that Guru, her Lord: "What is the name of this woman?
Jaigīṣavya said:
"This woman of excellent complexion is indeed Tuṃbarukābhijñā."
Formerly, while Nārada was engaged in ascetic penance together with Tumburu,
Viṣṇu appeared here for the benefit of Nārada.
Indeed, he who performs a bath here attains the supreme goal;
for all human beings, a bath here is difficult to obtain in the Kali age.
Bathing here for human beings is not the fruit of minor austerity;
having bathed there, drunk [the water], and given gifts, one is freed from all sins.
Returning once more, that goddess bowed down to Śrīnivāsa;
on that day, O beautiful one, she gratified the brahmins with offerings.
Having reached Svāmipuṣkariṇī, the virtuous and highly fortunate lady lit lamps on the steps; with rows of lamps,
she immediately gratified the Lord of Gods, Śrīnivāsa, the teacher of the world.
When the following day arrived, [he went to] the unsurpassed Śakratīrtha;
that purifying tīrtha is remembered as being in the upper region known as Kapila.
Having bathed there, O highly fortunate one, she should thereafter bathe him herself;
there is the Viṣvasena lake, which destroys all sins.
Thereafter, O highly fortunate one, she went there and beheld the sacred bathing places of the five weapons; she performed her ablutions in them.
Above that, there should be a sacrificial fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) which is difficult to ascend;
and in front of that, upon it, is the Brahma-tīrtha, which grants liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

Above that, however, is the meritorious sacred site of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), which yields excellent fruit; for each of those sacred sites, the merit increases tenfold as one proceeds further upward.
And who indeed here is worthy to describe the majesty of these?
At the *ṛṣi*-tīrthas, that maiden performed supreme austerity.
Having performed supreme austerity until my own incarnation,
she abandoned her body through the practice of yoga in the house of Jāmbavat.
Born as one named Jāmbavatī, she grew up in his household;
her father, Jāmbavān, then took that maiden [as a wife] for Rukmī. O Lord of Birds, she is this very Anantārā, my wife.
For who else on earth besides me is able to describe this supreme narrative of the great mountain Veṅkaṭādri?
Lakṣmī indeed always prepares the food offering for Veṅkaṭeśa, and Brahmā worships him constantly; such is the conclusion of the scripture.
One should not mock men who eat the food offerings (naivedya).
If one lacks the excellence [of the prescribed ingredients], then items such as jaggery (guḍa) and the like may certainly be accepted as the food offering;
of this there is no doubt. Otherwise, one will become a denizen of hell.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a god superior to Śrīnivāsa.
Having yourself cooked food such as that prepared with ghee and so forth,
you should partake of a meal only after offering it as *naivedya* to Śrīnivāsa.
This which has been told to you, O Lord of Birds, is supremely secret;
it must not be spoken to anyone because of its secrecy, O best of birds. Hereafter, I shall explain the gradations [of excellence]; listen, O Lord.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Various Pilgrimages Undertaken by Brahmā’s Daughter," in the glorious *Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa*.
In a previous creation, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa and wife of Rudra, [cast off] her own body at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having been released, she was born from Menakā, indeed from the presence of Hemavān, the upholder of the earth.
O Lord of Birds, she who was formerly Pārvatī, the wife of Rudra, or Vāruṇī by name, the wife of Śeṣa— she,
that great woman devoted to her husband, has arrived in a dual form to sport with Balabhadra.
She who is named Śrī is possessed by the entry of Indirā; her second image is in the form of a cloud.
Indeed, when Viṣṇu performed penance together with him (the Lord), she was in the form of Śeṣa.
At that very time, the goddess Vāruṇī, the wife of Śeṣa, performed penance for the sake of pleasing Indirā.
Then Indirā, being pleased and well-disposed, spoke to Vāruṇī, the wife of Śeṣa.
O auspicious one, when Rāma, endowed with a portion of Viṣṇu, appears on earth,
you, united with me through my entry [into you], shall be known as Śrī and sport with Balabhadra.
"You shall attain [perfection]; there is no need for further deliberation on this," she said, and having spoken thus, she indeed departed for the world of Viṣṇu.
Having received the praiseworthy name "Śrī" from a portion of Śrī Lakṣmī, she became the wife of Śeṣa in the world.

Whenever Īśa lifts up the vast [earth], then Rāma, at the confluence of the Śrībhidā, always brings about the satisfaction of Ramā; indeed, her very manifestation (āveśa) removes the association with the darkness of the three qualities.
She who is Revatī, the daughter of Raivata, is Vāruṇī, the wife of Balabhadra;

she who is named Sauparṇī is the wife of Bala. O Lord of Birds, know that those three are twice as inferior as the wives of Viṣṇu, and ten times as inferior as those of Rudra, Śeṣa, and the others, O grandson.
Garuḍa said:
Vāruṇī, the fair-browed daughter of Revata, attained the state of being the wife of Rāma for the sake of sporting with him at all times;
thus Vāruṇī exists in three forms, while Pārvatī, the wife of Rudra, exists in two forms as the consort of Śeṣa.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, it is heard by me that there is some similarity between the low-born Jāmbavatī and Śeṣa; tell me the reason for this.
"And likewise, O Lord, Rudra is always superior to Umā by many qualities;
thus have you spoken, O Blessed One, for the sake of my certain understanding, O Master. (GarP 3.28.11)
Revatī, Śrīyutā, Śrī, Vāruṇī who is the form of Śeṣa,
Sauparṇī, and Pārvatī— these three are the most excellent among the hundred daughters of Śeṣa.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Madhusūdana, it is heard that [this occurred] somewhere;
O Kṛṣṇa of noble vows, tell me the cause of this for your disciple."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Lord of Birds, having understood that there is equality between Jāmbavatī and those other excellent ones, it arises from the descent of the Supreme.
Indeed, even the quality of those who are inferior is dependent upon those who are superior;
it is said to be "more than a hundredfold" precisely to illuminate this fact.
O Lord of the Vidyādharas, understand what I say exactly as it is and not otherwise;
I shall now speak of those born immediately after him—listen, O best of the noble Kāśyapas.
Among the fourteen Indras, he who was the seventh was Purandara;
for the wise declare that the bodies of Vṛtra and others are called "fortresses" (pura).
Because he shatters that [fortress] with his thunderbolt, he is therefore called Purandara;
among the fourteen Indras, Mantradyumna was the sixth.
Since the great lord of mantras,
the god Mantrānanda, shines forth, therefore in this world both Mantradyumna and he are indeed one and the same.
O best of birds, Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, was an incarnation on earth of Mantradhūmna,
Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Ananta, and Indra.
Pārtha, endowed with four [qualities], is proclaimed as Indra himself;
yet, O Arjuna, there is also a distinction regarding Vāyu in the fourth [quality].
The monkey named Vālin was known as Purandara;
and from the Lunar dynasty arose the wise King Gādhi.
He is remembered as the incarnation of Mantradyumna and the father of Viśvāmitra;
because he sustained with his intellect the cows known as the Vedic mantras, he is so called.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, he was called Gādhi; for that purpose, there appeared on the earth a son of Ikṣvāku renowned as Vikukṣi.
He himself became an incarnation of Indra for the very purpose of serving Hari;
and because he specifically perceived Hari within his own belly, he was always known as Hari.
Therefore, this son of Rāma named Kuśa is always renowned in the world of mortals as Vikukṣi; he is proclaimed to be none other than Indra himself.
Because he was fashioned by the sage Vālmīki out of *kuśa* grass,
the lord who brings joy to Jānakī is therefore called Kuśa.
Indradyumna, Purandara, Gādhi, Vālī, Arjuna,
Vikukṣi, and Kuśa— these seven are proclaimed as the Indras.
He who is the son of Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, is proclaimed as Kāma himself;
he bears the name Pradyumna because his form is of an intensely radiant nature.
Bharata, the brother of Rāma, became the very embodiment of desire upon the earth;
because he carried out the command of Rāma, he was therefore named Bharata.
Kāma, who presides over the discus, is remembered as Sudarśana;
Brahmā himself is the son of Kṛṣṇa, namely Sāṃba, the son of Jāmbavatī.
The descent of desire is to be understood; there is no doubt about this.
Skanda, who is the son of Rudra, is proclaimed to be desire itself.
Because he constantly leaps upon his enemies, he is known as Skanda;
or rather, he who is Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā and lord of birds,
should be understood as an incarnation of Kāma— of this there is no need for doubt.
Sudarśana, Parama, Pradyumna, Sāmba,
Sanatkumāra, and Sāmba— these six are the Kāmarūpakas.
Furthermore, even Indra and Kāma are inferior to Umā and the others by ten degrees;
between those two, however, Kāma is considered inferior to Indra.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the ego (ahaṅkāra), known by the name Ahaṅkāra;
it should be understood as a portion of Garuḍa, ten times inferior to Kāma and Indra.
Immediately after that, I shall speak of the subsequent [births]; listen with a concentrated mind, O Lord of Sages.
By hearing this, one attains liberation and is released from great sin.
Even Niruddha, the son of Kāma, is proclaimed to be distinct from Hari;
yet he himself became Rāma’s younger brother on earth in order to perform service to Hari.
He is renowned as Śatrughna because he utterly destroys his enemies;
and from Pradyumna was born Aniruddha, the son of Kṛṣṇa.
He is indeed pervaded by the three forms beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa;
thus the high-minded Aniruddha is to be known as having two forms.
Rati, who is proclaimed to have two forms, is the wife of Kāma;
the daughter of Rukma, Rukmavatī, is proclaimed to be the wife of Kāma.
Because she was endowed with excessive radiance, she is remembered as Drugmavatī;
that daughter of Duryodhana, Lakṣaṇā, is remembered as Rati.
Kāṣṭhā was the wife of Sāmba; she endowed him with auspicious marks (lakṣaṇa), and thus he became known on earth by the name Lakṣaṇa, even though he was born from corrupted seed.
Thus, Rati, the wife of Kāma, is known to be of two forms.
Svāyambhuva Manu, the son of Brahmā, was equal to his preceptor;
he was born through the royal dharma of Viṣṇu in order to please Hari.
Bṛhaspati, the high-souled preceptor of the gods, had three incarnations, O Lord of Birds.
During the incarnation of Rāma, Bṛhaspati became the one named Bharata, joined by an infusion of the Lotus-born One.
Having caused the monkeys, who were incarnations of the gods, to cross over, he recounted the divine deeds of Śrī Rāma;
for this reason, he became known by the name Nārada, having attained the status of an *aṅga* (limb/minister) of Lord Rāma on earth.

From the wife of Agni, the wise one was born as Brahmā, possessing the conceit of Brahman; and Budha, the son of Candra, was also born.
Indeed, he took up the entire multitude of kingdoms with his intellect and held them; therefore, he obtained the name Budha.
And thus was the high-souled Abhimanyu born from Arjuna in the womb of Subhadrā.
Joined with portions of Kṛṣṇa, Candra, Yama, the two Aśvins, and Hara,
Budha— the son of Candra and the lowest of those born from Svāhā— is a devotee at the lotus feet of Lord Viṣṇu.
The wife of Aśvin, named Uṣā, is celebrated as being of the nature of Name (nāmātmikā);
she is to be known as inferior to Budha, and Svāhā is ten times more inferior than her.
The wife of Nakula was the daughter of the Magadha king, the daughter of Śalya; she was the wife of Sahadeva.
Indeed, both of these wives of the Aśvins, along with Uṣā, worship the primordial Viṣṇu who possesses six qualities.
Therefore, O King of Birds, she is known by the name Uṣā. Listen now to what follows, O Great-souled One, for I shall speak.
Then the power, whose essence is the earth, always moves slowly;
therefore it is named Śanaiścara (Slow-Mover), and these are the ten lowest states of Uṣā.
Puṣkara is to be known as the self of karma; Śani, Ratha, and Yama are considered [his attendants]. The Puruṣa named Kiñcinmātra is the leader, having ten [attendants] below him.
Since he constantly sports at Puṣkara, bringing delight to Hari,
he is therefore celebrated in the world by the name Puṣkala.
O Lord of Birds, listen as I shall describe those dharmas that bring pleasure to Hari:
having risen at the time of dawn, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
O Bird, one should perform the salutation of Tulasī and remember Śrī Viṣṇu;
and at the time of voiding feces and urine, one should remember Keśava, who is of the nature of the lower breath (apāna).
At the time of purification, one should worship Hari as Trivikrama, who drinks from the Gaṅgā;
at the time of brushing the teeth, however, one should worship Hari as the inner controller within the moon.
O bird, at the time of washing the face, one should remember Mādhava;
and likewise, while scratching the cows, one should remember Hari, the upholder of Govardhana.

O best of birds, one should always remember the Beloved of the Cowherds at the time of milking the cows, and when the fruits of one's birth and actions— earned through infinite merit— have reached full maturity.
Indeed, for men there is always auspiciousness from touching cows; therefore, no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
In that house where there is never an excellent cow, and in whose courtyard there is no sacred *tulasī*, [that house is desolate].

In whatever house there is a great festival for the gods, yet in which there is no hearing of Viṣṇu’s name, one encounters suffering and the like through association with that place; therefore, one should never even touch such a person.
They say that the birth of one who is devoid of the touch of a cow, who does not know the milking of a cow,
and who is devoid of the tending of cows, is useless.
For one who does not give even a mouthful of fodder to a cow, nor provides for her nourishment, there is no destination at all; he is remembered as being like an outcaste of the village.
While Vatsya was drinking from her breast, he should remember Bālakṛṣṇa;
and during the churning of the curd, he should remember Hari as the support of the churning-stick.
At the time of bathing with clay, one should remember Hari as Varāha;
and likewise, when applying the sectarian marks (puṇḍra), one should remember the twelve [forms] beginning with Keśava.
While holding the mudrās, one should likewise visualize the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
as well as the lotus, the Nārāyaṇī mudrā, and the Kruddholkā and others.
O best of birds, one should remember Śrī Rāma at the time of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā),
and one should remember Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda at the time of the ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
During the five oblations beginning with *prāṇa*, one should meditate upon Aniruddha and the others;
however, at the time of offering food and other items, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva.
At the time of the *apośana* rite, one should remember Hari who has entered within the wind;
at the time of putting on one's garment, one should remember Upendra Hari.
While wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one should remember Nārāyaṇa known as Vāmana;
and likewise, at the time of waving the lamp (ārārtika), one should properly remember Viṣṇu known as Paraśurāma.
At the time of the *apośana* rite of the *vaiśvadeva*, during other fire-oblations and the like, and when applying the sacred ash (*bhasma*),
one should remember with devotion and supreme reverence Nārāyaṇa, the Rāma known as Jāmadagnya.
At the time of taking up the water from the sacred ford three times, one should remember Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Vyāsadeva in sequence;
and at the time of lifting the water from the conch, one should always remember the form of Mukunda.

At every morsel of food, O Lord of Birds, one should practice the recollection of him named Govinda; at the time of taking each individual mouthful, one should indeed properly remember Acyuta with pure food.
While eating vegetables and the like, one should always remember Dhanvantari at the proper time; likewise, while enjoying food offered by others, one should properly remember Viṣṇu as Pāṇḍuraṅga.
Upon eating *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter), one should indeed properly remember Kṛṣṇa known as Tāṇḍava;
and upon eating curd-rice, one should always remember the supreme, ancient Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Likewise, at the time of consuming milk and rice, one should properly remember Śrīnivāsa and Hari;
and when eating food cooked with excellent oil or ghee, one should remember Vyaṅkaṭeśa.

One should indeed remember Bālakṛṣṇa amidst the beautiful fruits of grapes, *sujambū*, plantain, mango, orange, and pomegranate, as well as the exquisite beauty of the finest plantains, coconuts, and *dhātrī* fruits.
At the time of drinking a beverage, one should properly remember Viṣṇu known as Nārasiṃha;
and at the time of drinking the nectar of the Gaṅgā, one should likewise remember Viṣṇu, the father of Gaṅgā.
At the time of departure, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, who has Tārkṣya as his vehicle, who is beyond all attributes (nirguṇa), and whose form is the universe;
and at the time of kissing one's sons and others, one should remember Kṛṣṇa himself, with a beautiful flute in his hand.
During the time of sexual pleasure, one should always remember Hari, who delights in the pair of breasts of his own consort;
and at the time of chewing betel, one should always remember Vāsudeva, known as Pradyumna.
At the time of going to bed, he should always remember Hari in the form of Viṣṇu known as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
at the time of sleep, he should remember the one named Padmanābha; and at the time of storytelling, he should remember Hari in the form of Vyāsa.
At the time of eating, one should remember Hari accompanied by the song of the flute; at all times, one should utter "Hari, Hari.
And at the time of plucking the sacred Tulasi leaves, one should indeed remember "Śrī Rāma, Rāma."
When cutting flowers and the like, one should properly remember Hari known as Kapila;
and during circumambulation, O Lord of Birds, one should always remember Hari who resides within the Gāruḍa [Purāṇa].
At the time of bowing to Viṣṇu, the God of gods, one should remember Viṣṇu residing within Śeṣa;
at the time of seeking good counsel, one should remember Nṛsiṃha; and one should always remember Nārāyaṇa.
When the fulfillment of one's actions is performed, one should properly remember Vāsudeva and Hari;
thus, actions performed in this manner become pleasing to Hari.
Puṣkara, the beloved of Hari, performed these correctly.

O Lord of Birds, from this very [account] that has been proclaimed, he who listens with faith to this incomparable narrative of Puṣkara will always be filled with devotion for the dharma that brings delight to Hari.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Secret of Reality," in the Brahma-kāṇḍa, the third part of the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa.
This glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa is now complete.
Thus the glorious Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa is finished.
